name: Preface
text:
Thirteen years after writing more than twenty texts that eventually resulted in the book Anarchocapitalism, in which I describe a free free market stateless society, I again felt the need to write a book. On its pages, I deal with the reasons why we do not live in such a society today, but above all, I propose - first a theoretical, then a practical - way how we could get closer to freedom. First, I identify how we lose our freedom (which typically occurs from childhood); then I derive the consequent logical effects on our civilization. Finally, I return to the individual again and present concrete practices of how we can liberate ourselves in the everyday of our lives.

I would like to appeal primarily to the reader for whom freedom is at least a somewhat important value; although it is not absolutely necessary that it be the alpha and omega of his life, I am speaking primarily to the one to whom it is not completely indifferent. For those who do not think about freedom or do not feel that they need it for something specific, I would rather refer to the book Anarchocapitalism. In it, I explain why a free, unregulated society is, among other things, significantly more effective in meeting the needs of those who live in it.

Today, many politicians flaunt freedom in their election campaigns. We read about it on billboards, hear about it on TV and on the Internet, and even make up parts of the names of political parties. For many of those who use the word, however, it is nothing more than a cheap way to appeal to voters; also as a result of this emptying of the concept of freedom, there is a centralization of society and an increase in the number of regulations and legal norms that aim to govern practically all aspects of our lives. How to get out of this legislative jungle?

Even if we were to admit that social change is not yet in sight, there are a number of concrete steps towards freedom that anyone who cares about can take today - despite external restrictions. Furthermore, I am deeply convinced that any attempt to change society by social engineering "from above" is most likely to fail, just like any central planning. Changes "from below", that is, in the everyday lives of individuals, are therefore the only functional tools for achieving freedom anyway. Want to know more about them? I want to share them with you on the following pages.

name: 1. Freedom
text:
Freedom is my lifelong theme; I've been researching it since I was a kid. I looked for it in democracy, various (centralized) utopias, enlightened monarchies (with simple legislation and draconian punishments) and in a small state, until about twenty years ago the desire for knowledge led me to study anarchism (primarily anarcho-capitalism). I strongly rejected it at first, until my search for arguments against it led me to (reluctantly at first) accept it. Thanks to this, I also discovered the first comprehensive definition of freedom that made sense to me: A person is free precisely when no one violates his negative rights. These are equivalent to property rights, primarily to the body (self-ownership), but also to all physical property. The so-called principle of non-aggression is based on respect for property; the latter consists in not initiating violence (not even in the sense of threatening such actions), and therefore in using physical force exclusively for defense. These are different ways to describe what we can simply express with the words: Live and let live.

The preceding paragraph discusses the freedom of the individual from oppression caused by other people. However, the more intensively I dealt with this issue, the less I found this - however fundamental and valid - concept to be sufficient, since it does not deal with the demons within ourselves. Is a drug addicted, unhappy, broken and hateful person free just because no one initiates violence towards them? In a sense, yes; however, despite the absence of external limitations, he may not have the determination to realize his purpose in life (whatever it may be). On the other hand, there are stories of people from gulags or concentration camps that were not broken even by sadistic jailers, with whom these prisoners could even sympathize. These and similar examples led me to the need to distinguish between external freedom (that is, the absence of the oppression of aggressors, which I wrote about above) and internal freedom (that is, the willingness and determination to do what really makes sense to a person).

In the beginnings of my research, although I perceived and felt inner freedom, I could not describe it more precisely; it was only after several years that I was able to formulate a satisfactory definition: Inner freedom means the absence of fear or the ability to work with fear when it is present. It is therefore not a binary quantity, but a scale - the degree of our fear (or inability to manage it) corresponds to the degree of our inner lack of freedom.

This concept is based on the belief that, ultimately, it is fear – whether of failure, pain, loss, the darkness within ourselves, or anything else – that holds us back from doing what we find meaningful and fulfilling. Although at first glance it may seem that there are other reasons, I believe that in the end, fear is always hidden behind them - for example, of material hardship, what others will think of us or ourselves, that something will not work out for us, how it will harm us or our loved ones, and so on. Those who are not afraid have no reason not to try to do something that fulfills them and gives them meaning. Even behind what may initially appear to be, for example, laziness, upon closer examination we find precisely fear (perhaps from discomfort). Since many people question this principle, I spent a lot of time analyzing the examples they used to try to disprove it; despite this, I am not aware of any (even hypothetical) situation in which some form of fear is not behind the causes of someone's resignation to fulfilling the meaning of life.

An attentive reader may have noticed that I am talking about the determination, willingness or effort to do something in connection with internal freedom, or rather the absence of aggression in the case of external freedom, while I am not at all concerned with the results of a free person's actions. Because I consider it important to distinguish between the freedom to act and the real possibility of achieving something in the real world. These states are commonly confused; for example, "What good is the freedom to travel if I don't have the money anyway?" The author of such a sentence may feel unfree because he does not have the means to fulfill his needs; however, I believe that confusing (lack of) freedom with (lack of) options or resources is rather unfortunate - we could then come to rather absurd conclusions such as that we are not free if we do not have a time machine, a teleporter, a dragon or a date with our idol.

We rarely hear someone say that they are not free because they can't do magic (or at least make beautiful music). More often we can hear someone complaining that their freedom is limited by a lack of (typically financial) resources. Why? Because we tend to constantly compare ourselves to others: Many people feel unfree when they cannot afford even a cheap holiday at home, while their neighbors travel around the world; At the same time, almost no one considers the fact that they do not have a spacecraft capable of interstellar flights as a detriment to their freedom, since no one (yet) owns one. However, if everyone had ships capable of intergalactic travel, they would easily begin to see even interstellar as insufficient. If someone finds the previous sentence hard to believe, they can try to compare the availability and quality of owner-occupied housing for young families today and a hundred (or several hundred) years ago; nevertheless, today's (albeit better) state is found to be completely intolerable by society as a whole.

If we want to understand freedom universally, we cannot derive it from where the grass is greener, whose neighbor's goat died - or, more generally, from the technological level of civilization and our socio-economic position in it. In other words, it doesn't make sense that the same abilities, resources, and opportunities make us free in a poor society (where we have, say, the only car) while unfree in a rich one (where we own the same car, but everyone else already has private helicopters); for that would mean that we lose our freedom just because others get rich, even if they otherwise did nothing to us and did not limit us in anything.

Similar examples can be used to illustrate the difference between real unfreedom and the feeling of unfreedom; it can also stem from the fact that we do not have the opportunity to fulfill our needs, even if we are free at the given moment. Even if we desperately want something that everyone around us has and we just lack it, we need not therefore be unfree; and it does not give us any claim to the property of others. People sometimes call for a "dignified life" and basically mean that they want to have similar opportunities and resources as those they compare themselves to; at the same time, they forget that the feeling of dignity comes from ourselves and from our inner set-up. Why should exactly the same conditions (for life, housing or anything else) be "decent" at one moment, but perhaps in a hundred(s) years from now only because the standard of living of other people has increased? At the same time, it does not have to be only about material goods; I would like to illustrate this with an example from my own life to show that I stand by my words, even when the going gets tough.

Some time ago, after a serious accident with twenty-five broken bones, I was confined to bed for several months, then to a wheelchair, and still sometimes need crutches; I will probably never get rid of the pain and I won't be able to walk or even run normally. I think I might see the situation as a restriction of freedom if I hadn't spent so much time studying it in the past. Since I had fortunately already experienced that my external freedom can only be violated by others, while the internal one can only be violated by my own attitude, I was able to feel free even with a broken spine, unable to even drink or defecate without help. This not only helped me in the given situation (my regeneration far exceeded all expectations thanks to my approach stemming from inner freedom), but above all in practice it confirmed the theoretical starting points that I present in this book.

But what if we long to fulfill our dreams, but lack the means to do so? I am convinced that if we are internally free, i.e. we are not held back by fear (for example of failure), and we have determination, we can always do our best to obtain those resources. This may not be successful, but if we act with the sincere belief that this is truly our path, we fulfill our life's mission. Of course, we have the possibility at any time to decide to go a different way, to start fulfilling completely different needs or goals; and even if we are not aware of them, we can start working precisely to reveal them. It means it's never too late to start - we can always do our best for what makes sense to us (even if we don't even know it at the time).

However, sometimes life is so difficult that our strength may not be enough. Then it can be tempting to reach for a shortcut, the abundance of which has unfortunately been normalized by the states. Where our willingness or determination to face fear is lacking, the paternalistic state comes in, like the devil in a moment of weakness, offering us a "solution" - tempting and easy; with one catch - someone else (but ultimately ourselves) will pay for it, and that's the price of freedom. We often hear people calling for freedom where they feel confident and on solid ground: Those who can make money usually ask for economic freedom; good shooters or drivers often reject restrictions on guns or automobile traffic. On the contrary, blanket regulations are typically demanded by those who do not feel strong about something: Former or quit smokers formed one of the strongest voices for a ban on smoking in Czech pubs; the poor keep demanding legislation to redistribute the rich's money and such.

We could observe the combination of both phenomena (the demand for legislative restrictions and freedom) a few years ago in the public debate about the regulation of social networks: Before Elon Musk bought Twitter, a lot of conservatives called for state intervention in the then progressive-tuned platforms; those of us who opposed that the market would solve the situation, then those in question sharply attacked - until the market really solved it - so that the same conservatives would then start rejecting the same state interventions, because the tables were turned and, among other things, because of the X network, the Republican candidate became the president of the USA.

I perceive a great difference between the principled advocates of universal freedom for everyone and the people who call for it only when it suits them as a means to achieve a certain (their) end. And although I wish it from the bottom of my heart to absolutely everyone, I fear that those who are willing to sacrifice (especially other people's) freedom for the promise of fulfilling their needs will eventually lose it (even for themselves) to a much greater extent than they expected; and they may not even be aware of it. Why is that so? And how to defend against it? Before we answer these questions, let's look at when and how we start to lose our freedom...

name: 2. Education
text:
For millions of years of the evolution of the human species, children naturally learned everything necessary for life from their parents and other members of the pack, later also of larger societies; a few centuries ago, however, a drastic change took place - the mass expansion of education. Today, we could divide a person's life in terms of learning into three stages: The first years after birth, he decides more or less on his own what he learns (typically he acquires speech, walking and other skills when he sees fit); then comes the turning point in the form of starting school (not to mention the fact that the current Czech legislation also imposes a mandatory year of kindergarten) - it is shaped in the critical years of adolescence at the discretion of teachers, respectively politicians and officials of the Ministry of Education; after finishing school, he returns to what he has been doing since birth - he decides for himself what he needs to know, be familiar with, or be able to do (including when and how he will learn).

Full autonomy in deciding the time, content, methods or intensity of learning (self) - so-called self-directed education - is of fundamental importance for every person. Thanks to self-management, he/she not only acquires new knowledge and skills, but above all becomes aware of responsibility for his/her education, and therefore also his/her entire life. This happens regardless of the method (and even the intention) of learning, which is ongoing. Although we cannot explain what and why we learn, and we do not even call our actions learning, it occurs (thanks to the neuroplasticity of the brain) in every moment of our waking lives (and probably even in our sleep). The more autonomous we are in this process, the stronger we strengthen our awareness of responsibility for our lives in addition to developing specific abilities; at the same time, we may not be able to describe such a thing or be aware of it at all, yet it inevitably happens - because we constantly bear the consequences of our decisions, and the less external influences enter into them (for example, orders and prohibitions from parents or teachers), the more clearly we perceive this principle.

As parents or teachers, thanks to life experiences, we sometimes know ways of learning that can be (at least for us) more effective than those we observe in "our" children; then of course we can share our experience with them, if they are interested. However, the problem arises when we start to elevate these experiences and methods (albeit time-tested) above the approach of others (perhaps much younger) and force them to learn as we see fit. Coercion tends to have negative effects on interpersonal relationships, however, if the given experience is suitably transferable to another person, it can help them to acquire a certain skill more effectively or faster. However, in no case can we avoid the fact that by limiting the autonomy of the person in question, we always delay at least a little from realizing the responsibility for our life. In other words – the more we suppress someone's freedom, the less we allow them to be responsible; not to mention the effects on his self-esteem - by imposing our solutions on him, we are showing him that his decisions are not well-founded, which can undermine his self-confidence.

Coercion does not only affect the psyche. It also negatively affects the effectiveness of learning, although, paradoxically, it is the fear of parents or teachers that the child will not learn something that leads them to suppress their autonomy. However, fear robs us of our inner freedom, which we discussed in the previous chapter, and clouds our judgment—we tend to overestimate the potential problems of not knowing or being able to do something, while ignoring the negative consequences of coercion. Economics describes the concept of opportunity cost; it follows from it for our needs that whatever we do, we lose the possibility of doing something else at a given moment. So whenever we force a child to learn something, he cannot spend that time learning what he would like. At the same time, everything that he learns from internal motivation, because he enjoys it or sees a different meaning in it, he absorbs much faster than if he does the same thing out of compulsion.

An outside observer may not have a good enough understanding of another person's learning process; and even if he knows him intimately or makes a living from pedagogy. As a kid, I spent a lot of time playing Dračí doupě (a Czech Dungeons & Dragons-style tabletop RPG) and Red Dragon (MMO strategy), which the adults around me didn't like to see. At the time, I was not able to explain to them - what I can only see in retrospect - that these games gave me far more in my life (whether in terms of communication, imagination, logical thinking or responsibility) than school. However, most people see games as an inferior form of education; and if they take them to their mercy, then only if they recognize in them something resembling the school curriculum. At the same time, they do not realize that we need much more in life, including the ability to find our own way. I myself tried dozens of games before I found the two that enriched me so much - and it is no coincidence that I spent thousands of (for me extremely productive) hours on them. We will probably never fully understand the learning process of others; and therefore even activities whose meaning we don't understand can be an important part of it (for example, I know a person whose self-development was key to not being able to tear himself away from watching short videos as a child, which paradoxically helped him a lot in later life).

In schools, we encounter almost exclusively three-quarter-hour blocks of frontal instruction; at the same time, there are countless educational models suitable for different types of people - for example, I best acquire knowledge by creating videos, writing texts, lecturing or dialoguing with people, which I had to figure out on my own (despite school - my attempts to discuss with teachers were punished there), while something completely different can work for each of the students in the desks (be it listening, moving, traveling, drawing or countless other methods). The reason why almost all schools choose only one from a whole constellation of learning styles is because of their centralization; it reduces the effectiveness of education, which we discussed above, but above all it suppresses our autonomy, which I would like to address further.

The government approves (irregularly, about once a decade) a national education program in which it formulates its vision of education; the current one is called Strategy 2030+ (it's free to download on the Internet) and it abounds with a lot of buzzwords describing what children should be led to do. One of the few things that really grants the child some autonomy in that document is the emphasis on critical thinking (although autonomy is mentioned in several places, but rather vaguely). However, there is a catch - there are a lot of contradictions in that text, which remain hidden to most readers (and probably also to the creators), because they were shaped by this educational system (albeit in its older form). I consider the following contradiction to be the most fundamental: In addition to critical thinking, the document also focuses on the transmission of values and attitudes (primarily democratic); but how can we lead someone to (arbitrary) values and attitudes without suppressing their critical thinking?

After all, critical thinking means that we form our own opinions based on working with information according to the principles of logic; in contrast, taking on (any) values is the exact opposite of such a process. If the goal of teaching is for the student to (not) adopt a certain attitude, then this goal is not compatible with the critical thinking of the person concerned; for this would mean that he would form his own opinion, which may be contrary to the desired intention. Either we try to give someone as much unbiased information as possible and let them make up their own minds, giving up control over what ends up happening; or we try to lead him to certain conclusions, but by doing so we try to deceive his critical thinking. The intention of the authors of Strategy 2030+ is most likely that pupils apply critical thinking only in certain areas, while in others they accept their values; paradoxically, this can be even more dangerous than the open imposition of certain attitudes, because those concerned may not be aware of it at all.

The 2030+ strategy is implemented in framework educational programs (mandatory for all schools); they state: »[...] the overall climate of the school [...] creates a democratic classroom atmosphere, serving as a "laboratory of democracy". In it, pupils are more motivated [...] to the possibility of participating democratically in the decisions of the whole, the community, the community. At the same time, they can not only verify for themselves the importance of following the rules [...], but also how important it is to take care of the maintenance of democracy, because crossing the border to anarchy or vice versa to despotism is a constantly present danger. This experience then develops the ability of critical thinking.« Here the contradiction is glaring – the authors of the text demand that the school be set up in such a way that pupils will learn the importance of democracy and the danger of anarchy, which they paradoxically call critical thinking. I would like to add that I am not discussing here at all whether democracy or anarchy is right or wrong; for now, I am only concerned with the fact that the authors do (declaratively) want to develop the ability of critical thinking, but they state it directly with an example in which the student should accept their preferred (pro-democratic and anti-anarchist) values, not form their own opinion.

However much the schools declare themselves to be apolitical, neutral, pluralistic and non-ideological, they are full of advertisements for the state; it tends to be included both directly in teaching, where demonstrable falsehoods are heard, for example, about everything that cannot exist without the state (property rights, firefighters, healthcare, the social system and the like - although we know contemporary or historical counterexamples), and also in the school environment - the portrait of the president and the national emblem hanging in classrooms in a visible place near the blackboard, in front of which children sit for many hours a day. How much do you think private businesses with child customers would pay to have their logo on there? And what resistance would something like that cause in society? I suppose a lot of money and a lot of backlash - simply because that form of promotion works; nevertheless, advertising for the state basically does not bother anyone (except anarchists), because it is "correct" to influence children in this direction.

I consider the worst thing about the entire education system is that it is compulsory - whoever does not enroll their child in school, the state threatens to take it away. There may be no neglect or even abuse; it is enough to have a different idea about education than the politicians and officials in the ministry. Imagine any institution other than the state threatening to kidnap people's children if they don't raise them as they order them to; we would probably describe something like that as monstrosity and barbarism. Why is it not only possible for the state to do this, but also why it is perceived as desirable by society? I believe that the systemic suppression of critical thinking is behind this...

name: 3. Indoctrination
text:
Where critical thinking is suppressed, there is room for indoctrination – that is, shaping one's attitudes and values so that the person accepts them and does not question them. It is a key tool for effective propaganda of various ideologies. Skillful indoctrination can be not only so subtle that we don't even notice it, but we may not even recognize the presence of any ideology; here we can consider it an integral part of our reality. When this happens, we then unwittingly become its spreaders by simply sharing our knowledge with others; the wonderful process of learning is attacked by this devilish virus.

While in the past the key to controlling the masses was primarily the dissemination of information suitable for the one who wanted to rule them, today manipulators have to deal with another obstacle - namely the huge amount of data that surrounds us. Even if we do nothing but consume content, we absorb only a drop of the sea of the Internet; we can't even imagine the vast majority. How do we decide what to pay attention to? In general, we ignore what doesn't interest us, but also what doesn't make sense; and this is exactly what good propaganda can use. If someone succeeds in indoctrinating us with an ideology in such a way that we don't even consider it an ideology, because it has become part of our reality, we will logically start discarding information that contradicts it, because it does not make sense to us. At this point, it's no longer an error of judgment, but a sensible way of working with data - there's so much nonsense around us that we simply can't analyze it all.

Before we get into the propaganda of the present, let's look at what people were willing to believe in the past - the pharaohs were gods, the sun rose due to human sacrifices, god punished natural disasters, witches caused disease, the devil had more power over masturbators, the brain of a savage (or woman) did not match the size or qualities of a white man's brain, slaves were things, while Jews were subhuman; and since these are myths that are at most thousands of years old, their bearers were biologically the same people as us (with the same potential to think) - they were only distinguished by the environment in which they grew up. First, it shows us how susceptible we are to succumbing to collective manipulation; and secondly, that if we have been uncovering the errors and delusions of previous generations on an enormous scale throughout essentially the whole of history (and we continue to do so all the time), we can be almost certain that the process is not over - we still believe a lot of them - and today's myths will probably appear as absurd in a few centuries as the above ones today.

When we live in something, we get used to it; it feels normal to us and it would be strange not to do it - whatever it is - from bowing to the king to going to the polls. And so today we can still see the propaganda of past regimes (for example Nazi or Communist). However, we are blind to the current one - it has become an integral part of our reality. From an early age we are taught to respect the flag, anthem, state symbols or constitution; but how can we think critically about something if we first learn to worship it? School creates in us positive emotional ties to certain concepts (such as democracy) and negative to others (such as anarchy) before we get the chance to form our own opinion, and sometimes even only (strong) feelings remain without any information: As part of one Free Port project, we asked random people what they thought of T. G. Masaryk - without exception they called him a good person and president; almost no one could answer the following question, why they perceive him that way (you can find the recording on the Internet).

I would like to illustrate the consequences of the indoctrination to which we are exposed using concrete examples from contemporary Czechia; however, they are all generalizable to at least the entire Euro-Atlantic civilization (and some worldwide). I will deal with the general propaganda of the state and democracy, as these are the strongest ideological campaigns that I recognize around me; at the same time, I do not yet want to address whether or to what extent they are justified, necessary, or even useful. So let's focus in the following paragraphs only on the indoctrination itself, not on assessing the specific values hidden behind it. I would like us to try to map for the time being the extent to which state and democratic propaganda influences us.

It is democracy that is one of the greatest models of today; our society associates with it freedom, protection of minorities, equality before the law, human rights and the like. Technically speaking, however, this is a government of the majority, which can easily decide to suppress the freedom and rights of various groups of people; and as long as it respects the results of unrigged elections, any atrocities can happen even in a completely democratic way, which few people admit. Democracy is commonly seen as a good by definition; the words democratic and undemocratic are therefore sometimes used as synonyms for good and bad - for example, when we hear politicians say that the actions of their opponents contradict democratic principles, it is often just a strong condemnation of something that may not have anything to do with democracy or elections at all. On the other hand, those who want to address a serious problem of a democratic society sometimes prefer to speak of "pseudo-democracy", "democracy", "would-be democracy" or "post-democracy", even though it is a democracy; but reviling it is so unacceptable that we prefer to choose other words.

In the previous chapter, we focused on centralized education and its national educational program. Imagine if I designed one that included the following goals, among others:

• develop the role of the school as a Christian institution,

• equip the student with the skills and knowledge to uphold and promote Christian values and attitudes,

• to develop the student's ability to act as a true Christian, to honor the Ten Commandments and to fully participate in church life. I suppose you could identify the indoctrination of Christianity in them if they were to be taught in schools. However, to quote something from Strategy 2030+:

• develop the role of the school as a democratic institution,

• equip the citizen [...] with skills and knowledge to uphold and promote democratic values and attitudes,

• develop the ability to act as a responsible citizen, take care of [...] sustainable development and fully participate in civic [...] life, do you feel the same way about this? I (today already) do (even if it took me many years); however, I am in the minority - although people (today in the Czech Republic) typically recognize and reject Christian indoctrination, they not only accept the democratic indoctrination, but often do not even see it, as it has become part of their reality.

State propaganda leads to cognitive dissonance: For example, most of us (declaratively) identify with the principle "live and let live", but only as long as someone does not live in violation of the applicable legislation - then all hell breaks loose, even if the person in question does not harm anyone - after all, we "know" that a decent person should respect the laws or try to change them if he does not like them (that "letting live" is suddenly no longer enough). Let us now leave aside whether or not there is a need to follow the legal order; I'm just pointing out the fact that you can't consistently demand that people obey the law while maintaining a "live and let live" attitude. These principles are contradicted every time someone does not follow the applicable legislation and at the same time does nothing to anyone, so he "lets" others live (for example, he makes brandy for his own use without the permission of the state). However, as a result of indoctrination by state propaganda, most people hold both of these opposing positions at the same time without realizing it.

Another example is freedom of speech - we learn in schools that we have it in our democratic society; but what does that mean? In theory, about so much that its boundaries are determined by legislators; in practice, it is restricted in Czech legislation by, for example, prohibitions on the dissemination (by the state) of classified information, approval of criminal activity, election campaigns forty-eight hours before elections, discrimination, promotion of certain movements, questioning of genocide (it also affects scientific research on the number of victims), defamation of certain groups, slander, libel, and so on. For a lot of people, free speech means that what they want to say isn't banned, or that it's okay to restrict neo-Nazis; however, for example, some passages of this book can fulfill the factual essence of approving criminal activity (I have already been summoned for similar texts). However, I don't want to argue yet whether or not it is right or necessary to limit freedom of speech; I point out that despite what we learn in schools, this freedom was suppressed not only by past regimes, but also by the current one (albeit to a different extent).

As a result of indoctrination, we are able to perceive basically the same behavior as acceptable or unacceptable depending on who is committing it; and even something as serious as murder. When someone attacks and intentionally takes another person's life, we normally think of it as one of the worst crimes; however, if it happens on behalf of the state, we perceive it completely differently. If a soldier murders someone in a war—even an offensive one—he is not typically considered a murderer; when something is done by the state, we view it differently than when the same thing is done by an individual. Yes, the person was "just following orders"; but what if a non-soldier defended himself like that? What if someone murdered because his non-military employer ordered him to? For the vast majority of people, such situations are incomparable; just like hundreds of years ago, there was a fundamental difference between murdering a slave and his master. Every time it is a murder of a person, but sometimes it is viewed differently according to what the given society is indoctrinated with; and this is true throughout history.

As I wrote above, the point of this chapter is not to judge the legitimacy of democracy, the state or its laws or the army; I tried to use various examples to demonstrate the consequences of indoctrination by state propaganda. If you have identified some of them in yourself, you can think about them and come back over time, perhaps even to those that you do not perceive yet; they can tell a lot about any strong emotions while reading. I have been spreading the ideas of anarchism for almost my entire adult life; and while they certainly take some time to explore, I often encounter an immediate strong rejection from people who have not previously known them. Even if I were wrong, those concerned did not have enough time to detect such a mistake; yet how many times before they even started to think about them, they were already clear (as I was, after all, when I first came across them).

name: 4. Obedience
text:
In previous chapters we have dealt with indoctrination by state propaganda; we are exposed to it from an early age in schools. However, if I were to ask what is the first thing we learn in school, what would be the most common answers? Read? Write? Count? I'm afraid that even before we can even dive into any of this, we have to learn (in a regular school) to obey; and to obey a complete stranger - a teacher. He or she determines when we are obliged to sit, what and how to do, what to pay attention to; and even often forbids us to fulfill basic physiological needs (primarily drinking, eating, excreting, but also others). If we obey him, he will reward us, while if we do not, he will punish us. Both the level of coercion and the severity of punishments can vary depending on the type of school; however, the basic principle remains the same (except for a handful of exceptional schools) – the child must learn to listen to the stranger who is assigned to him.

In the beginnings of the expansion of mass education, the needs of the army were strongly taken into account for its concrete form (especially in Prussia after the Napoleonic defeats). The educational system required strict discipline, hierarchy, uniform frontal teaching, a fixed class schedule, management by ringing the bell, age segregation, supervision in the corridors, a ban on speaking without prompting, public rewards and punishments, evaluation, grading and, above all, compulsory attendance – i.e. tools to remove autonomy and strengthen obedience. Although today's education formally declares different goals - for example, the development of independence, creativity, critical thinking or responsibility - it uses identical means to achieve them, which are, of course, in conflict with these goals; and while there are cosmetic changes, the basic principle remains the same. It's like trying to eat soup with a fork - I can bend its prongs in different ways (that's about how effective the current "reforms" of education are), but the liquid will still flow through them; the solution is to take a spoon - however, this would mean a real reform - i.e. discard the concept of classes, evaluations and the like, but in any case above all coercion.

Having gone through this educational system, we have become accustomed to it; we consider a lot of phenomena in it to be normal, even if anywhere else they could at least raise doubts in us. Let's focus, for example, on the behavior of teachers towards children: What if a boss demanded of a subordinate, or a classmate of a classmate, for example, demanded that he drop everything and stand up when he enters the room? Most of us would probably consider this bullying; not to mention having to ask permission to go to the bathroom and a lot of other humiliating procedures that we have to undergo during adolescence, when our self-confidence, self-worth, self-love and overall integrity are formed. Even the fact that many generations before us went through something similar does not reduce the destructive effects on our psyche.

It is true that many schools try to moderate the humiliation of children, which they have the support of the Ministry of Education and mainstream society to a certain extent; however, even though the form of the educational process has changed in recent decades, its essence unfortunately remains the same – pupils remain in a subordinate position to teachers. Beating with a cane or a key or staying after school and copying the same sentence over and over gave way; however, this does not mean autonomy for children - they have to do what is required of them anyway - only "softer" forms of manipulation are used for this (public praise and reprimands, grades, etc.). On the one hand, I'm really happy for everyone who doesn't have to kneel in a corner in shame for punishment; on the other hand, I perceive another danger in these "reforms" of education - the obedience and subordination of pupils has been given a gloss, so it is no longer so obvious (both to children and adults).

I assume that the vast majority of readers of this book attended one of the schools based on the obedience of children under the guidance of adults (although the means of coercion and the degree of authoritarianism may have varied); and since it is difficult to imagine a workable alternative as a result, I would like to briefly describe one. I teach (and learn) at the Ježek bez klece (Hedgehog Without a Cage) school, where we don't tell children (or adults) when and what to do - we leave everyone full autonomy; you won't find evaluations, punishments, division into classes or management hierarchy here (the founder of the school has the same voice as a six-year-old when deciding on anything - from personnel issues to economic matters to time management), we always look for consensus, and above all nothing is compulsory (not even attendance, and yet - or rather because of that - children like to come early in the morning and leave late in the evening or sleep over). Unfortunately, this is not always in accordance with valid Czech legislation; nevertheless, we are living proof that it is possible to educate yourself in a different way than the state mandates. I will write more about the Hedgehog without a cage in one of the following chapters; I only mention it here to show that while I question the requirement of obedience on a theoretical level, I also offer a tried and tested alternative that works in practice.

I criticized direct state propaganda - and considered it to be the main cause of unfreedom in our society - long before I joined Hedgehog without a cage; I still stand by that criticism, but daily contact with children growing up in a respectful environment, where interpersonal interactions are based on mutual voluntariness, has led me to believe that there is an even worse enemy of our freedom than direct state propaganda - namely obedience. In addition to the fact that, according to my observation, "our" children are better at saying no and guarding their boundaries (which, among other things, makes them more resistant to sexual and other predators), they often do not even understand why they - or anyone else - should be ruled; they didn't grow up in a hierarchy and nobody told them what to do and what not to do, so it's natural for them to make decisions about their lives. I am convinced that the autonomy of the individual is the basis of a free society; on the other hand, obedience—required in ordinary schools—leads to unfreedom.

Why is obedience so dangerous, you ask? Let's recall Milgram's experiment: In 1963, Yale University published an ad asking for volunteers for a learning experiment for a reward of $4.50 (about 1,000 CZK / $45 today after inflation); they were "randomized" into the roles of "teacher" and "student" - however, in such a way that the "teacher" was always the respondent, while the "student" was portrayed by an actor on whose body the experimenter placed electrodes, which the "teacher" was convinced could be used to deliver electric shocks (of gradually increasing intensity starting at 15 volts) for wrong answers as part of a "research on the effect of punishment on learning"; even when they weren't live, the "student" played his part convincingly - screaming in pain, kicking the wall, etc., until he (feigned) passed out at 300 volts, a point reached by three-quarters of the "teachers" (albeit the buttons were marked with signs like "danger: severe shock"), with the majority continuing (under the instruction that the passed out silence was the wrong answer) after 15 volts to the end of the scale, i.e. up to 450 volts. The experiment was repeated many times with similar results; these depended on the physical proximity of the "teacher" and the "pupil", but also on what authority the participants considered the one giving them instructions - they listened to the scientist in the white coat rather than the "common man".

In addition to the effects on the individual lives of the obedient, we can also observe societal consequences; anarchist Howard Zinn aptly described them by saying, "Civil disobedience is not our problem. Our problem is civil obedience. Our problem is that people all over the world obeyed the orders of leaders; and because of that obedience, millions of people were killed." For he himself, as an obedient soldier, murdered many people, but unlike most of his comrades, after the war he revisited the places he had previously bombed; there he found out how much the information of the locals differed from that which he received from his commanders, but also from that communicated by the army to the public. Apparently this experience also made him an anarchist; his fascinating life story is easily found on the internet.

We often hear about how many victims Nazism, Communism or various wars are responsible for; but we rarely imagine that Hitler, Stalin and other rulers would be essentially powerless without millions of obedient ones. Obedience is behind more deaths and more suffering than all of Nazism and Communism combined; yet it is mostly seen as a virtue and we are rarely warned against it – on the contrary, from time immemorial we have been scaring our offspring with stories of the terrible things that have happened as a result of someone disobeying (from Adam and Eve to disobedient kids). That's why every time I hear the lament that a child "can't listen", I sincerely hope that it's really true and that they never learn; because I consider teaching children obedience to be one of the worst things we can do to them. However, I don't want to remain wishful thinking; I see every day spent in the Hedgehog without a cage as my small contribution to the fact that the results of the next repetitions of Milgram's experiment can be a little less terrifying and that there will be more people who refuse to kill others just because someone orders them to do so.

However, this effort is opposed not only by state education, but also by authoritarian regimes, whose leaders are very well aware of the importance of (dis)obedience. It is no coincidence that perhaps every totality (including historical ones) organizes various collective activities from mass celebrations, rallies, parades or military parades to work brigades and military exercises to spartakiades or gymnastic performances (for example, Arirang in the DPRK); in addition to controlling the population (you can see who participates and who does not), it shows individuals their smallness and trains obedience. In contrast, what strengthens individuality in people or awakens emotions leading to disobedience tends to be suppressed; whether it is sexuality (especially in the Middle Ages, but also in modern-day totalitarianism, it is taboo), certain musical genres (rock and jazz were basically banned by all contemporary authoritarian regimes) or other art (mainly avant-garde, experimental, modernist or abstract) - in short, everything that leads to spontaneity, unrestrainedness, independence, and thus undermines obedience.

Valuable lessons for our everyday reality flow from what rigid totalities show us on a massive scale: People can be controlled very effectively through their bodies - our personality is inevitably shaped in terms of (dis)obedience, whether it is military exercises and Spartakiads, passionate music or animal sex; however, whether you force someone to sit in a desk all day and talk only after logging in, or whether you allow them to move around as they want and need, has a similar effect.

name: 5. Adultism
text:
Human history is interwoven with the oppression of various groups of individuals; these may be defined by gender, race, religion, sexual identity or preference, or other characteristics. The cause of such oppression is typically prejudices that we easily see and condemn in others, while we often do not perceive our own; and when they do, we often don't even find them harmful because they help and protect us. The very existence of prejudice has its origins in the evolution of the human brain; thanks to them, we are able to quickly categorize and interpret stimuli (albeit at the cost of a certain distortion of reality), which we sometimes need for survival. It only matters to us how we work with them; they can be a good servant but also a bad master.

When we learn about the oppression of different groups in schools, the teaching typically deals with either the past or some extreme or threat on the fringes of society; it practically never addresses contemporary systemic persecution. With the normalization of any form of repression, a certain society-wide blindness to it also arises; paradoxically, we then pay more attention to minor or past problems (because they are easier to see, since we do not live in the given environment) than to big and current ones (which remain hidden from us, because we are unable to create a distance from them). We discussed a similar phenomenon in the chapter on indoctrination – when people get used to something, they accept it as an integral part of their reality and stop dwelling on it.

As an example, the Declaration of Independence of the United States can serve us, which states: "We hold as self-evident truths that all men are created equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable rights, among which are life, liberty, and the pursuit of personal happiness." When Thomas Jefferson wrote this sentence, his favorite coffee was most likely brought to him by one of the hundreds of slaves he "owned"; and he probably didn't find it strange at all! Although this was a very intelligent man, who probably meant his words sincerely - after all, there was nothing to prevent him from phrasing the sentence differently and excluding slaves from it - he simply did not even consider slaves as people, so he had no reason to choose other words; he too was most likely (despite his multidisciplinary education and encyclopedic knowledge) affected by the blindness of his time and environment.

Whenever a group is systematically persecuted, people in that society have their reasons why it seems right (or at least necessary). Their motives for oppression always appear to be reasonable in the context of the time - otherwise they would not be accepted by the majority - typically it is an objective observation from which conclusions are derived that we find to be misguided only in retrospect. For example, we can see that evolution has endowed women with a higher emotional sensitivity than men (due to communication with children) or dark-skinned people with higher time preferences than light-skinned people (the closer to the equator, the darker the skin and less need to plan to survive the winter and therefore worry about the future); today we take these as simple facts that most of us don't draw any major conclusions from, but in the past people considered women's emotionality a reason not to allow them to build a career or vote, while African-American slaves were assumed to be unable to fend for themselves without their master. As absurd as it may sound to us today, these were very convincing arguments of the time; and since our brains have not evolved biologically since those days, there is no reason to believe that we should be immune to such thinking today.

I am convinced that although our society works to alleviate many forms of oppression (and has already basically dealt with some of them), we still do not see the most oppressed group of people in this way; we have a blindness similar to that of Jefferson towards slaves - and that when we think about children. Not only do we forbid them to act legally (we say they are not competent), to work and to do business, the police return them to their parents' homes (or to an institution) if they decide to leave and live their own lives, but we also do not recognize their self-ownership (they cannot decide, for example, about their treatment and other essential matters) or their right to privacy (pedagogues have reporting obligations, but even therapists have to share the content of sessions with parents). The exercise of power by adults over children – their discrimination – is called adultism; our society is permeated with it, even though it might not be. Does that sound absurd? Maybe; but that is certainly what the equality of slaves sounded like centuries ago, and the equality of women decades ago.

I don't dispute that children have less experience than adults and their brains are not yet fully developed, so they typically cannot see the consequences of their actions as well; just as I don't question a lot of objective differences between genders, races, and the like. The question is: What conclusions do we draw from this? Our society has set uniform age limits, on the basis of which it denies certain freedoms to all younger people, regardless of their personal capabilities and abilities; at the same time, it would be possible to approach each individual individually, which we do anyway in the case of adults, whose competence, for example, to act legally, we also sometimes limit - but always on a case-by-case basis, never across the board (for example, according to IQ or educational attainment, which can be just as "good" reasons as lack of experience in children). Of course, it could mean more work for judges, for example; but seriously is this a sufficient argument why restrict someone's freedom? I believe that one day universal age limits will be viewed similarly to separate entrances for blacks and whites.

I am not suggesting that every child is capable of understanding and entering into a complicated contract, choosing treatment, driving a car, or having consensual sex; after all, many of them can't even read yet, some can't even speak. However, I personally know many people who are quite competent to perform certain actions, but who are prohibited by law because they have not reached a certain age; to say that we will not allow them so that they may not be abused is not unlike the belief that a slave cannot take care of himself without a master. If we really want to protect children, not have power over them and make decisions about them, let's allow each of them to act according to their individual possibilities and abilities; of course, this does not exclude the possibility of abuse, which would have to be assessed on a case-by-case basis (as in the case of adults), not across the board according to the age limit.

Part of the Czech constitution is the Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms, the first article of which establishes the equality of rights of all people, the seventh the right to privacy, the ninth prohibits forced labor, the eleventh enshrines equal property rights for all owners, the fourteenth freedom of movement, and articles eighteen to twenty-one guarantee all citizens, without exception, the right to participate in the administration of public affairs through elections, petitions and other instruments. Yet we legislatively restrict children's privacy (for example, parents have access to their medical records), own more property, prevent them from moving and force them to work (during compulsory schooling), not to mention the impossibility of public administration. Let us now leave aside the expediency of such measures; let's note that although this document does not restrict children (on the contrary, it explicitly states the same rights for everyone), almost no one even thinks of interpreting it that way - just like Thomas Jefferson, it probably did not occur to him that "all men" could include slaves. This is also why I believe that we suffer from the same blindness to systemic oppression as our ancestors; this belief is also supported by the fact that children's freedom stands outside any social debate, including the one about discrimination based on age (it only addresses the problems of old people).

The improvement of society's approach to oppressed groups typically does not occur on the basis of the discovery of new facts or knowledge, but by changing the paradigm - i.e. the generally accepted view of the world; for example, the differences between genders or races are still the same and well-known, even if people's attitudes have changed significantly even within the last century. So I don't expect adultism to disappear from our culture on the basis of new scientific discoveries, nor do I expect existing knowledge to be challenged - statistically there really are vast differences in cognitive and other abilities between children and adults; however, our views and the conclusions we draw from the available knowledge may change. Unfortunately, this means that we need to work with our own emotions rather than facts, which is more difficult for most people in our civilizational framework - this is also related to the education in which we are taught almost exclusively about the external (factual) world, while the internal (mental) remains largely unnoticed.

In the previous chapters, I described how restricting an individual's autonomy affects his self-confidence and ability to make competent decisions about his life (even though it is the alleged incompetence that is the reason for these interventions); in this one, let's think about what it means to be part of a group over which society exerts its power. One might argue that a person's race, gender, sexuality or nationality remains the same while age changes, so in the end everyone is the same; and he would be right, but it also implies that we all start life in a subordinate position. A child whose freedom is restricted by someone all his life (even if he means it well) cannot even imagine what it is like to be a being equal to others, because he has never experienced it; then when he grows up and the legislation grants him the same rights as others, we cannot expect that there would be any fundamental change in him - in the best case, he will gradually become aware of his autonomy and adopt it little by little, in the worst case, he will resort to seeking external guidance...

name: 6. Leadership
text:
If I had expected everyone to agree with me on the harmfulness of adultism and the obedience of children, I probably would not have felt the need to write this book at all; since you are reading it right now, I do not expect this agreement, but nevertheless I hope that you will at least agree with me on the question of the very existence of these phenomena in our civilizational framework (even if most people consider them necessary, or even desirable) - we begin our lives in a subordinate position. This manifests itself most markedly in school, which, however, basically everyone went through, so that the overwhelming majority of parents accepted as normal - and subsequently adopted - the behavior with children described in the previous chapters, with the result that we were exposed to it as children both at home and in the entire society formed by (former) schoolchildren.

Unfortunately, the subordination of children is not only anchored in legislation; it pervades interpersonal relationships. There are a number of things that adults commonly say to children that are considered "rude" (giving instructions, evaluations, reprimands, yelling); a general example implemented in the Czech language and etiquette is asymmetric ticking. Intrusions on privacy, control of "free" time, forcing things to be done, sometimes even choosing friends are all practices that reinforce inferiority. I consider interference with bodily autonomy to be the absolute worst, from forcing food to physical punishments to involuntary physical contact (hugging, giving or holding hands, kisses from relatives, etc.) - these are ways to reinforce in children the (sometimes lifelong) subconscious belief that other people (especially adults) can make decisions about their bodies without consent, which not only makes them extremely vulnerable, but also strengthens their subordinate position.

Many people unconsciously expect that a controlled person growing up obediently at the bottom of the social hierarchy will become healthy self-confident and responsible at the stroke of their fifteenth or eighteenth birthday; but obedient children typically grow into obedient adults. It is true that sometimes they rebel; in such cases, however, they usually become "rebels without a cause" - rather than searching for themselves and their meaning, they turn to resistance against everyone and everything. One way or another, there are only a handful of individuals living among us who have no problem saying yes to what they need and no to everything they don't want; while they too often had to devote a lot of time and effort to freeing themselves from the patterns adopted in childhood. Other people - the majority of society - at least to some extent try to meet the expectations of those around them rather than doing what they themselves consider fulfilling and meaningful.

This phenomenon was investigated by the psychologist Philip Zimbardo in his famous Stanford prison experiment: In 1971, he selected twenty-four of the many dozens of registered volunteers who, based on questionnaires and psychological examinations, he evaluated as the most emotionally stable, blameless, healthy and without previous problems with addictions, aggression and the like; he divided them into twelve "prisoners" and twelve "guards", who together were supposed to simulate prison for two weeks. The task of the "guards" was to control the "prisoners", but they were not allowed to use physical violence to do this; all were dressed in matching uniforms, "prisoners" were addressed only by numbers, while "guards" were addressed as "Mr. Correctional Officer". The experiment had to be terminated prematurely after six days, as the conditions in the "prison" became so cruel and the "guards" so sadistic that there was a risk of permanent consequences for the participants - several "prisoners" collapsed (the first after only one day) and left the experiment, despite the fact that they were young students who received 15 dollars a day (almost 2500 crowns today after inflation - which, by the way, is more than double compensation, which is currently normally paid by the Czech state to people convicted on the basis of a miscarriage of justice and held involuntarily in real prison without the possibility of leaving).

Philip Zimbardo and his colleagues who studied the Stanford experiment identified as one of the main causes of unexpected cruelty the so-called de-individualization - that is, the state in which an individual loses a sense of his own identity (and thus also responsibility for his actions), thereby becoming an obedient part of a larger collective; in the case of the attempt, this was especially enhanced by the uniforms or the way of addressing "guards" and "prisoners". I consider a very interesting part of the experiment when the "prisoners" were visited by their families; although some visitors experienced unusually strong signs of stress, agitation, anxiety, and fear from their loved ones, which disturbed and outraged them, they were relatively easily calmed or silenced by the experimenter as an authority figure. I also find it remarkable that the "prisoners" were convinced that the experimenter assigned the most physically powerful volunteers to the role of "guards", but this was not true (he decided by lot and both groups were made up of people of approximately the same physical constitution); in my opinion, this distortion could have been caused by associations with situations that the persons in question experienced in their childhood, when (older) adults treated them similarly.

So the Stanford experiment shows us not only the pathological behavior of the oppressors; we can also observe changes in behavior and above all in the perception of the controlled. There is no reason to believe that in the case of pupils - and all children in general - similar phenomena do not occur, although of course they may differ in specific manifestations, degree and scope (Zimbard's experiment exposed the participants to stronger repression than is normally experienced by minors, but on the other hand, only for a few days). We all learn by imitation, in connection with which I would like to quote Gabriela Ježková, the founder of the self-directed Ježek school without a cage: "Do not do to children what you do not want adults to do to you." – the way we treat the youngest determines the future shape of our society, because they will grow up and start to shape it over time.

Those who learn to listen to their parents and teachers at a young age are likely to have a tendency to seek some form of guidance even after they leave the school and home where they grew up. It may not feel that way at all, because it will no longer be about direct education, but rather about defining boundaries and creating an (often illusory) sense of security resulting from the fact that someone has things under control - for example, a policeman, judge, official, politician. With regard to state indoctrination, which we dealt with in one of the previous chapters, it is no coincidence that this role is typically played by state representatives. For some people, it may not be about his specific representatives, but about the abstract idea of the state as a powerful entity protecting individuals from all kinds of uncertainties in the world (this is sometimes accompanied by a long-term dislike of individual rulers combined with the belief that we cannot do without them).

If a suitable leader is not available, the company can create one. When we think of Nazi Germany, for example, the question often arises as to how Hitler managed to manipulate so many people; he was certainly a charismatic speaker, but that is not enough in my opinion - such control requires the cooperation of the controlled. Hitler did not have a fixed vision at first, but he was frustrated and angry; so he began to publicly vent his ideas, some of which may not have elicited any response from the recipients, but others did - resonating with their emotions - and so the future dictator gradually developed them, gaining more and more support. I believe that this power-obsessed man did not invent National Socialism, which he would then present to the people—already finished; I believe that it was the joint work of a leader and a leader-hungry society. The cruelty of the resulting regime did not stem only from the nature of the Reich Chancellor, but above all from the desperation of his subjects, to whom they gave him full rein. After all, even today in politics, the one who has a clear idea and vision is at a significant disadvantage compared to populists, who formulate their ideas according to the reactions of their recipients.

The main purpose of this chapter is to question the widespread view according to which only their (higher-ranking) representatives are responsible for all evil committed by various regimes, while we perceive the "common people" as victims of "those at the top". On the one hand, I am convinced that it is always a joint work of all involved - even "pawns" who are "just doing their job". Above all, however, I believe that if "ordinary people" are victims, then not primarily of autocrats, but mainly of the educational system and adultism, as a result of which they not only seek leadership, but even actively participate in shaping the image of their leaders. This process is probably inherent in every regime; however, it acquires particular strength in a democracy where the rulers are dependent on the broad support of the citizens.

For the sake of completeness, I do not want to omit that the phenomena described above are not only the result of education and upbringing, but also to a certain extent of human nature; evolution has probably equipped us with tendencies to lead and be led. However, the fact that nature gave us something in the wine is not an argument that we necessarily act according to it even today; after all, we usually don't resolve conflicts with physical force anymore, and we don't want to give way to procreative instincts without the consent of the other party. Although I cannot exactly separate the influence of environment from genetic makeup, I have no doubt that at least education plays a significant role; not only because of the theoretical arguments that I present in this book, but also because of daily contact with a lot of self-directed children from the Hedgehog without a cage - their experienced patterns regarding obedience and authority are diametrically different from the majority society, which would not happen if they resulted only from human nature.

name: 7. Authority
text:
Every person we meet in life has some knowledge, skills, abilities or experiences that we do not possess; and so it commonly happens that we trust someone more than ourselves in certain aspects. We believe that a car mechanic can fix a car, a surgeon can fix a human body; we don't have to understand their fields, our trust is based on the knowledge of the world available to us - we could, for example, see the results of their work, give someone a recommendation or proof of education. These people become (voluntarily accepted) authorities for us; it is a completely natural process, and absolutely essential for the functioning of all humanity, because the concept of the division of labor stands and falls with it. If we don't want to go back to the trees, we need authorities. One might be confused by such a sentence from the pen of an anarchist; however, the following paragraphs should more than clarify it.

In the nineteenth century, the anarchist Mikhail Alexandrovich Bakunin dealt with the issue of authority; he wrote: "If I bow to the authority of experts [...] it is because their authority is not imposed on me by anyone [...] but by my own reason." So he did not mean blind obedience; quite the contrary: "When it comes to shoes, I recognize the authority of the shoemaker; about houses [...] I consult the architect. [...] I listen to them freely and with respect for their intelligence, character and knowledge, but always reserve the right to criticize and reject." Let us note in particular the freedom to disagree, disobey, leave or perhaps choose another authority, if we deem it appropriate. We can come to such a conclusion by ourselves and with the help of other people (for example, experts); however, the final decision remains only with us - even if we delegated it to someone else, it was still us who decided on such a solution. It is not an absolute trust in the infallibility of others, but our own judgment; even though we have at our disposal the opinions of experts of various specializations, in the end we always make choices according to our own discretion, because no one but ourselves can be an expert on our life.

Since no one is infallible, no authority can be absolute - not even in a narrowly defined field. Although we are all generally aware of the limitations of human knowledge, we often act contrary to this awareness; in every expectation of unconditional obedience lies an implicit assumption of someone's infallibility (otherwise there would be no need to always follow their will). Questioning authority should therefore not only be taboo, but on the contrary even strongly desirable; this is how we push the boundaries of our knowledge. If any authority becomes unquestionable for us, we suppress ourselves and fit into the role of its instrument. I consider it important to point out that the authority in this sense does not have to be only an individual, but also an institution - although many people are willing to acknowledge the possibility of a particular judge or politician making a mistake, they are also proud of their unshakable faith in justice and democracy (however, this is also dangerous and destructive, just like the deification of a certain person).

Thus, authority is never absolute (everyone makes mistakes sometimes), universal (there is no one expert at everything), but also immutable over time; since we choose it based on current knowledge, it can change with new information - either because we educate ourselves in something, or someone else becomes an authority for us, whom we consider (again based on our own discretion) to be more grounded. Not to mention that even if someone were right a hundred times, it says nothing about the relevance of that truth to our lives; the doctor may know the negative effects of lack of sleep on the human body, but only we ourselves can ultimately judge whether and why it is (not) worth staying awake in a particular case. If we approach (voluntarily accepted) authorities with the knowledge of the above, they can be very useful to us (and probably even necessary for survival itself). However, since the vast majority of us have been trained to obey, I believe that it does no harm to remind ourselves of these insights from time to time and look for various experienced unconscious patterns in ourselves - whether towards automatic submission or "rebellion without a cause".

It follows from the previous paragraphs that actually everyone recognizes some authorities; perhaps even unconsciously – every time they trust the driver of the means of transport they get into, or the producer of the food they already eat, and so on. Since this trust forms the fundamental pillars on which our civilization rests, and we constantly benefit from it, we understandably have an interest in sharing it with our closest ones - which for the vast majority of parents are "their" children. Then, in an effort to provide them with the best possible life, they sometimes forget that meaningful authority comes from competence; a healthy relationship with it is based on one's own judgment and voluntariness. We do him a disservice by teaching someone to accept authorities he did not choose for himself; even if it benefits him in any particular case, it makes him more vulnerable overall to those who seek to exert their power over other people (even if they do not do so with malicious intent).

This vulnerability can be exploited by charismatic fraudsters; we typically think of various sectarians or charlatans, but it also applies to pressure traders, fanatical conspirators, toxic superiors, coaches with a savior complex, and generally anyone who can take advantage of insecure people, in whom they first instill a sense of inferiority and then offer the illusion of a solution - often in the form of some type of (perhaps even short-term) dependence on the manipulator or their product or political party. He instills fear in those he wishes to control; they then, as a result, lose their inner freedom and become obedient. At the same time, their external freedom need not be violated at all; there is no need to threaten them with violence, let alone commit it against them - frightened people often submit (perhaps financially, but it can also be other types of submission) by their own decision.

The next level of abuse is represented by forcefully imposed authority; the victim is threatened with physical violation of property rights (in the worst case to the body, i.e. self-ownership) if he does not submit to her will. In the case of children, we typically think of bullying classmates or domestic abuse; for adults, then, most often, for example, various assaults, robberies, rape or intimate partner violence. Primarily, these are attacks on external freedom, during which the internal one does not have to be violated (although it often is).

Authority may therefore be natural and voluntary; such does not violate anyone's freedom and is apparently necessary for survival in human society. Another type of authority comes from manipulation and fear; it comes from the limitation of inner freedom. And finally, there is authority (by violence or the threat of it) imposed; it flows from the trampling of external freedom. Manipulative and violent authority often come hand in hand; their combination then suppresses the autonomy of the individual at all levels. Note that with every acceptance of authority a hierarchy is created; this can be voluntary and typically useful (in the case of natural hierarchies created on the basis of recognition of someone's wisdom, abilities, knowledge or competences worthy of following - which everyone decides for himself), but also coercive - or directly imposed - and harmful (where any manipulation or coercion is needed, there is clearly a lack of internal motivation based on personal conviction). It is often (though not always) true that a healthy hierarchy is informal. If formalization is needed (perhaps even just in the form of somehow named roles or functions), I personally at least ask myself the question, what is the reason for it, and I pay increased attention to such a situation.

Any formal hierarchy is not necessarily immediately dangerous if it rests on the consent of all involved and thus does not infringe on anyone's external freedom. However, I am convinced that an excessively hierarchical society will gradually lead to the suppression of the inner freedom of those who are in those hierarchies - the time spent listening to orders "from above" cannot be used effectively at the same time to find one's own happiness and meaning. This is likely to cause further hierarchization; at first perhaps voluntary, but over time probably also (by force) imposed on those who do not want to participate, which means an attack on their external freedom. Indeed, internal and external freedom are closely related: Internally free individuals typically do not feel the need to oppress others from the outside (whereas the unfree rather do, because they fear them); and an environment free of repression, in turn, strengthens inner freedom (while oppression disrupts it by inducing fear). If we want to prevent future oppression by disrupting the voluntary hierarchies around us, we need to do so peacefully (through dialogue, example, self-management, competition and the like) without interfering with the external freedoms (i.e. property rights) of others; otherwise, our efforts will not only be in vain, but will also become counterproductive, which we will discuss in the following chapters.

Mandatory hierarchies, to which people must submit in order not to be harmed, represent, in my opinion, the greatest evil that mankind has yet created. Individuals (even the most depraved sadistic serial killers) simply do not have the means to commit what a lot of "ordinary people" who are "just doing their jobs" in a hierarchical organization can do. Why does layout matter so much?
