Because if these individuals organize themselves differently (either in a competitive environment in the free market, or perhaps in communities making decisions by consensus), with a probability approaching certainty they will not commit such atrocities as if they are subject to a distant central authority to which they can transfer responsibility for their own actions in their heads. Unfortunately, I am far from talking only about the Soviet Union or the Third Reich or some medieval churches; we still have giant forced hierarchies maintained by force today and we all live in them - they are states.

name: 8. State
text:
The state represents the most widespread and strongest form of imposed authority today. When I speak of a state, I mean any (at least somewhat hierarchically organized) entity that usurps a monopoly on violence within a territory (of considerable size) that it does not own. So it doesn't matter what it's called (I don't consider a non-violent entity to be a state, even if it was called that), but what it actually does (a private company physically controlling a large area without the owners' permission is a state for me). Let us note that whoever obtains the exclusive power to decide when and how others may (not) use violence can establish an arbitrary monopoly, i.e. also in the field of law and dispute resolution; from this follows the possibility to codify any rules as laws and establish (purely from a position of power) what is and what is not legal - regardless of ethics. An overly complex system of legal norms often creates various illusions in people (for example, that it exists for their good and safety); with sufficient complexity, it is possible to create the impression that it is something other than the "right" of the stronger (although it does not act).

In the past, states ruled mainly on the basis of direct, crude threats; simple subjects who opposed the sovereign (for example, in matters of taxes, military levies and other duties) awaited a cruel and painful punishment. Back then obedience had to be enforced by exemplary displays of force, as the rulers did not have a centralized education system that could "explain" to children that they were running the country in their best interest and that without the state we would all kill each other. Today, public displays of brutality would be counterproductive, as the vast majority of people have been convinced at an early age that "we are the state," which is far smarter from a marketing point of view than the king declaring, "I am the state." Over the past centuries, the technologists of power have done a lot of work, as a result of which it is no longer necessary to control the masses by the threat of torture or public executions; managed not only to convince them that they need leadership, but even to hide from them the ever-present threat of violence for the disobedient - which only a handful of us will feel (fortunately not as strongly as in the past), officially not in the name of a tyrant's whim, but for the "good of the whole society".

Although much has changed over the millennia of the existence of states, their essence remains the same: They set rules (even if the way they are created evolves over time) and force people to obey this order by physical violence (or the threat of it); unfortunately also individuals who do not harm anyone with their actions and only look out for their own. Violation of the law is punished, not interference with the freedom of others (which sometimes goes hand in hand, for example when a private person steals someone's property, but not necessarily, for example, if the state does the same as part of taxation, expropriation or nationalization). Let us not forget that, however sweetly phrased, legislation is ultimately always enforced by physical force (ie the "right" of the stronger); whoever does not submit to the decision of the state court (however unjust or senseless it may be) will be forced to do so by force, possibly put behind bars, sometimes even killed if he resists. Let's remember this every time we hear politicians defending new laws by saying they will give someone a "life with dignity"; it is always at the expense of all those who are deprived of their human dignity by the police and security guards.

So prisons are not only filled with those who have wronged someone and victims of miscarriages of justice; they are also inhabited by people who really broke the law, even though they did nothing wrong to anyone - they just didn't have enough strength to defend themselves against the state. Many more, however, submitted to the hegemon of power only to avoid such punishment; this is also why I consider state power to be illegitimate and unethical. In addition, I find it very inefficient; economics correctly teaches us that and why monopolies are expensive and unproductive - only the vast majority of (state) schools "neglect" to cite the state as an example of the largest monopoly. Of course, it also applies to him that without the need to try for consumers' money (taxes are mandatory even for those who are not satisfied with the state's services), he has no motivation to be economical or pro-customer; in addition, it runs into a problem of economic calculation that cannot be solved in practice - the central planner does not have at his disposal decentralized information scattered throughout society, so he cannot make informed decisions about the lives of people living in it. If you would like to read more about this issue, I can refer you to my book Anarchocapitalism, where I address the impossibility of economic calculation in central planning not only in general, but also give examples from many fields; and I am not neglecting the ethical level of state intervention either.

As the complexity and complexity of relationships in our society increases over time, states respond by churning out more and more laws to cover and describe this diversity in vain; the result is the uncontrolled growth of the legislative jungle in which we are all forced to live. In 2010, the Department of State Analysis of the Institute of State and Law of the Academy of Sciences of the Czech Republic estimated the number of currently valid standards in the Czech Republic at 1.6 million, while in 1990 it was "only" half a million, with their number rising steadily from year to year. Based on this trend, it can be extrapolated that there are about two and a half million laws, standards, decrees, regulations and regulations in force at the time of publication of this book. Ignorance of the law is no excuse, but we live in an environment where complete knowledge is completely out of the question; and not only for lawyers, but also for legislators and their advisers. Yet people sometimes argue against anarchy by saying that society is too complex to be left in anarchy; but isn't this the best argument against the government, since it is not in the power of more self-sufficient politicians to grasp and manage this complexity?

However, even if the state were most efficient (which it certainly is not), this does not legitimize its domination or violent coercion; if so, it would mean that whoever discovers something that works purposefully (and perhaps even optimally) gets the right to force it on others. With non-state entities, we clearly see the senselessness of such behavior - on the one hand, good solutions do not need to be imposed by force (people are happy to accept them themselves), but above all, it would require some arbiter who will decide for others what is best for them; if the author of the given discovery himself fit into this role, everyone would be aware of his bias and no one would take such an approach seriously - unless, of course, he does so with his own strength, which is not worth resisting too much. A lot of people therefore prefer to submit and retroactively rationalize this choice (the rules apply to everyone the same, without obedience chaos would reign, it is a tax on a civilized society, it is not so bad after all - there are countless "arguments" with which state oppression is defended, although any other, even much weaker, no one would defend with them); it's probably less painful than facing the absurdity, plus we've been brought up to do it.

Even the very financing of the state is ethically extremely problematic - almost all of its income is taxes. We are taught in schools that these are service charges; but if this were really the case, there would be some connection between the payment and the drawing of the consideration. However, paying taxes is not a condition for using state services; people pay a set amount of tax typically to avoid being penalized (if this were not the case, taxpayers would not pay so much attention to opportunities to pay less, while tax authorities would not expend so much energy to control them). We pay for non-state services to benefit from them (therefore there is a link between their price and quality); however, if we do not pay the state what he measures, he will ask for more, under the threat of violence - imprisonment, or even shooting, if we defend our freedom. If anyone other than the state declared that it provides services for which everyone must pay a price set by it, it would seem absurd to us, and if, in addition, it started threatening non-payers, then probably also reprehensible; so why don't we apply the same standards to the state?

There are also non-state organizations with a similar financing model - namely the mafia; they also provide services to people (most often the sale of goods prohibited by the state, the Japanese yakuza improves their PR and charitable activities) and also collect taxes, although we use the word protection money for them. Although taxes and protection money work on the same principle (those who don't pay will be punished - even if from the mafia other than from the state), they are deliberately named differently; states try their best to present their threats in the least aggressive form possible. On the other hand, mafias, which, unlike states, do not have an educational system available to convince us throughout our childhood that their activities are something more than organized crime, on the contrary, they need to appear terrifying; that's why they bet on brutality and their punishments tend to be harsher (in addition, they don't have taxpayer money to build and run prisons). Thus, there are differences between the state and the mafia, but mainly in the strategies of exercising power; however, both organizations initiate violence against the disobedient simply because they oppose their will, even if they otherwise do nothing to anyone, and enforce obedience through threats.

The states pulled off a masterstroke in the field of propaganda; they used the natural love of "their" citizens for the country they live in to identify with it - and not only with it, often also with the language, culture and other roots that they include in their signs and other symbols. Most people probably agree with the sentence already mentioned at the beginning of this chapter, namely: "We are the state." This naturally means that if the state should be bad, then logically we must be bad too; if the state is a criminal organization, that makes us criminals too. I can think of no better way for an organization to ensure that whatever it does is justified; it is not surprising that people like to use a double standard for the actions of the state and other entities (for example, the mafia) if they have been convinced that they are the state.

Although the form of the state develops over time and even today there are various types of governments and political arrangements, their very essence remains the same violent regardless of the specific regime (although this violence is no longer so straightforward, on the contrary, it is hidden behind various euphemisms and institutional processes); the rulers never stopped exercising their power by the "right" of the stronger - although the strongest individual is no longer considered the strongest, but perhaps the one with the "right" origin (nowadays rarely) or with the largest number of votes in elections (more often).

name: 9. Democracy
text:
In our civilizational framework, democracy has become the most common form of government; this can appear today as the least unfree way of leading the state, since the non-democratic regimes of today limit the freedom of "their" citizens even more. I wish I had as much confidence in this as the endlessly quoted Winston Churchill, who jokingly called democracy the worst form of government except for all the others (that we've tried so far); her rock fans tend to shorten the quote by the part in parentheses, even though it also belongs to it. As wise and profound as this may sound, let's note that the same can be said by a supporter of whatever system of government they happen to live in - and it will probably seem true to everyone (except the regime's opponents) (because they typically feel that what they live in has evolved beyond everything else).

I consider the biggest problem of comparing (modern) democracy with other state arrangements to be its relatively short duration; in most countries we are talking about only a few decades, for the pioneers even a longer period of time, but universal suffrage (and still not for children) has existed for around a hundred years at the most. At the same time, in all democracies without exception, we can observe an increasing amount of regulations causing the decline of freedom over time. I see the cause in a phenomenon that I have called the death cycle of democracy: Politicians promise voters various benefits - safety, social security, and the like - which they sometimes fulfill, however, thereby creating citizens more dependent on the state (either the recipients of the promised gains, or the civil servants who provide them); they then have an even greater tendency to vote for politicians who promise to expand the public sector. A self-reinforcing feedback loop is created (a growing state creates the need for further growth). This can be prevented by not giving those dependent on the state the opportunity to vote in elections; but this would mean the abolition of universal suffrage. So the freest countries today are undoubtedly democratic; however, this form of government lasts only a short time in them, while it already visibly strengthens the state and suppresses the autonomy of the individual. What's next? I hope for freedom; I just don't think we can break through to her.

In the chapter on indoctrination, we discussed that and why people identify democracy with the (general) good; it is therefore not surprising that they consider it to be the opposite of totality, which is not entirely true. Democracy (rule by the majority) is the opposite of dictatorship (rule by a narrow group or individual), which is not the same as totalitarianism (a state trying to regulate all aspects of citizens' lives); and although totalitarianism is typically established by a dictator, there is nothing preventing voters from voting against freedom in the long term (which they persistently do anyway). However, something prevents them from voting against democracy - just as the leading role of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia was anchored by the fourth article of the constitution before 1989, today's Czech constitution prohibits the change of the democratic regime in several places (articles one, five and especially nine), so the Ministry of the Interior blocks the establishment of non-democratic parties; anarchy is also unconstitutional, of course. The constant curse of freedom (which also happens in the constitution) accompanied by its inexorable erosion reminds me of the constructive enthusiasm of the socialists at the turn of the 1940s and 1950s, replaced by the rough sobering of the 1960s; I am afraid that democracy does not happen to go through similar phases - only longer ones.

Sometimes we hear that this or that politician is dividing society; but I am convinced that nothing divides it so much as the very rule of the majority, and its legal power to impose its will on the minority. In a truly free country, if people have different opinions, they don't have to threaten each other in any way - everyone can live their own life. However, in a democracy, a different opinion is a potential danger, as it can be enforced by force with the help of the state apparatus. Not to mention that when I need to get something done within the democratic process, the most effective way is not to open a dialogue with the one who can do the most harm, but to get as many (yet undecided) people on my side as possible; this is a general feature of all democratic systems - not only those imposed by the state, but also voluntary, for example within companies, communities and the like (I consider them legitimate, although I personally do not prefer them; I prefer to seek consensus of all participants, which, although it takes longer, leads to mutual understanding in the long term).

Democracy's winning strategy is populism; a politician who brings his own fixed ideas, opinions and attitudes is disadvantaged by them - the more he has, the less room he has to adapt to the results of public opinion polls. Nevertheless, populism tends to be seen as a problem by supporters of democracy; but a populist without his own ideals, always responding only to the voice of the people, can best represent their will. If we have doubts about this will, then we should also doubt democracy as such, which is not socially acceptable; therefore, people commonly defend it while preferring to turn a blind eye to certain aspects of it.

Viktor Orbán, who for over fifteen years has won about half the votes of the Hungarian electorate in every election, and therefore the majority of parliamentary seats, can be used as an example of a European politician who is perhaps the most described as a populist; this gives him the opportunity to control the media (including state media), use them for his propaganda and thus maintain his power. However, far more resources and media power than the Hungarian prime minister uses to make himself visible are still used to promote the state and democracy as such (and even in schools). Critics of the Hungarian prime minister see the pernicious influence he has when his opposition is not given enough space in the media; however, they are mostly unable to see that the same effect can be achieved by unilaterally informing about the state and democracy almost exclusively from the mouths of their supporters.

The existence of states is sometimes defended on the grounds that people are not capable and mature enough to govern themselves; if this is true, how can the same individuals be competent to elect their representatives? If they need the state to protect them, who will protect them from manipulation in election campaigns? At the same time, politics attracts the power-hungry; and anyone who has ever witnessed the happenings in political parties has probably noticed that even in quite small (and perhaps non-parliamentary) ones there is a rough struggle for power - those with sharper elbows and the ability to make an impression get to the top, while the authenticity and sense of fair conduct of politics within the party is at a disadvantage (just as loyalty to ideals harms them in front of the voters). Democracy therefore creates the conditions for the rule of powerful all-powerful populists; this does not mean that people with other characteristics cannot also rise to power, but it is less likely.

Although the results of elections can affect society (which I described above, for example, with the example of the death cycle of democracy), an individual's vote most likely has no effect; except in cases where a politician wins a mandate by a single vote (any individual voter could not go to the polls and it would not affect the result at all). So it doesn't really matter who you vote for, or if you vote at all; except for extremely unlikely cases in which a single vote decides on a representative - this sometimes happens in municipal elections, nationally in the Czech Republic never before, worldwide really quite exceptionally, and anyway that seat had no influence on the overall distribution of forces in the parliament - with the only exception in 1961 in Zanzibar, when the result led to a deadlock and new elections (which were already decided by more votes). If no one who voted in this African island nation more than half a century ago is reading this book, I can assure every reader that if they had never gone to the polls, they would have been governed by the same people; The Czechs and Slovaks also said that they would not even change the distribution of seats in the parliament, which is almost certain to apply to all subsequent elections as well - it probably doesn't matter at all whether and to whom you cast your vote.

Although I am only stating the facts in the previous paragraph, this is one of the most controversial theses that I am bringing into the public space. For similar statements, I have received death threats, countless insults and labels from a Russian cockroach to a neo-Nazi and a communist to a traitor, unfortunately not only online, but also in person. This whirlwind of resentment is typically accompanied by not-so-logical reasons why we should vote; most often that if many people resign from the election, the result will be disastrous. On the one hand, this may not be true (it depends on whose voters it would be), but above all, the (non)choice of an individual does not change the decisions of others - so their potential resignation can hardly be an argument for casting a vote in the ballot box (and, moreover, lower voter turnout increases the slight chance of an individual to influence the result, so it should be rather positive for voters). The unusually high intensity of the personal attacks caught my attention and made me wonder where such strong emotions come from in people. After many conversations with them, I have come to the conclusion that this is a defense mechanism to prevent them from accepting that something they have been doing all their lives could be useless - and above all, it would mean that their power to influence democracy is only illusory.

Defenders of democracy often criticize "irresponsible" citizens for voting based on their first impression of a politician rather than reading his party's program; but voting "responsibly" means spending a lot of time studying not only program statements, but also economics and other fields, not to mention assessing the credibility of pre-election promises, while the "reward" for this is nothing but the negligible (in)ability to influence anything; therefore, the criticized action is actually a rational use of limited resources (especially time).

In my opinion, democratic elections fulfill four basic functions: First, they move us from freedom towards totalitarianism (a growing state creates dependent citizens who vote for its further growth). Second, they divide society (people with different opinions are a danger if they can democratically impose them on us). Third, they give individuals the illusion that their vote is making a difference (although one vote basically never makes a difference; although activism and getting more votes can make a difference). And finally, fourthly, they create the appearance of the legitimacy of the state (but the will of the majority does not give anyone the right to use force against a minority; if it did, we could excuse the non-state oppression of a smaller group by any larger one).

name: 10. Statism
text:
Statism is the belief in the state; it is the most widespread world religion today. Unfortunately, Czech does not have a similar expression for the deification of democracy; therefore, in this chapter I will take the liberty of expanding the term statism and using it to denote the worship not only of the monopoly on violence, but also of the rule of the majority - in our society they usually go hand in hand anyway and show many common features. Although on a general level I consistently distinguish between faith, i.e. the inner conviction of an individual, and its institutionalization, which I call religion, in the case of statism the two terms somewhat merge; for the state itself is an institution based on violent coercion, so belief in it cannot in principle be a mere personal matter of the given person, as it involves demanding obedience from others (if not, it would no longer be a state according to the description from the previous chapter).

Like most religions, statism has different churches (in the form of individual states); they have their sacred symbols (flags, insignia), places (palaces, monuments), texts (constitutional documents, founding declarations) and songs (marchs, hymns), holidays (celebrations of victory, formation), celebrations (parades, military parades), relics (standards, crown jewels), officials (politicians, officials), symbolic gestures (salutes, laying of wreaths), saints (honored by statesmen, national heroes) and ceremonies (elections, coronations). These analogies may seem laughable or exaggerated, but few of us have ever been taught in life (especially in childhood) that the flag is not a piece of rag, the anthem a common song, the crown jewels are of "incalculable value," or have not been led to respect state symbols; moreover, in most countries they are defined by law and enjoy special legislative protection that limits freedom of expression (defamation of state symbols is punished to varying degrees).

While statists may not believe in any supernatural being, their thinking about the state often defies logic, largely ignoring any available information that challenges belief in the state, and typically refusing to confront their religion with it when they do notice it. An example is the entire Austrian school of economics, from which comes a lot of knowledge that forms the foundations of today's economics (subjectivity of value, marginal utility, opportunity cost, time preference and the resulting interest theory or methodological individualism), however, all conclusions questioning the state (the impossibility of economic calculation in central planning, business cycle theory) are simply neglected by the educational system (and then also by the entire public) - although they have never been refuted and for the last-named discovery they even won Friedrich August von Hayek Nobel Prize.

Because of the statism that results from the indoctrination (especially of children) by state propaganda, which we discussed at the beginning of this book, we are unable to see the state as other entities. Most people tolerate him for what they wouldn't forgive anyone else, trust him where they would normally doubt, let him do the otherwise unthinkable and, above all, do what he tells her (or at least what she thinks is right). Unfortunately, the impact of such thinking goes beyond these believers; for their religion also includes a strong belief that others should follow the same principles - otherwise they are often hostile or even aggressive towards them, or at least consider them suspicious or even dangerous. This setup keeps society in constant obedience – much like punishments. These fall on a handful of non-conforming individuals, while the belief that submission to the state is moral and virtuous keeps essentially everyone under constant social pressure and mutual control.

In the previous chapters, we could reflect on specific examples - how diametrically different most of us perceive taxation and firing or soldiers killing for the state in wars compared to hired killers committing similar acts privately. Even if we notice it on a mental level, it certainly does not mean that our perception will change. If these were positions consciously adopted on the basis of logical judgment, it would perhaps be easier to reassess them, but this is a religious belief that is instilled in us from a young age - it cannot be simply thrown away. I myself have observed and actively worked with these cognitive distortions for almost half of my life, but I don't expect to ever completely get rid of them. Every time, when I "dismantle" some layer from the upbringing of the dogmas experienced, sooner or later I discover another one - more subtle and hidden a little deeper, possibly manifesting in a different way or in other areas of my perception of the world.

We encounter various manifestations of statism all the time; let's look at politicians, for example: Who among us considers the current legislators or government ministers of their country to be so wise and trustworthy that they would voluntarily come to them for advice in life and then follow them consistently? From how unflattering politicians are commonly spoken about, I judge that few people. However, when the same MPs make laws (far more binding than any advice), the vast majority of us consider it reasonable to follow them, although they do not hold their creator in the slightest respect (in fact, on the contrary). Or how big a threat we already (quite rightly) consider the collection of data by private entities (to whom we can simply not give it); on the other hand, with the state, not only does it not bother almost anyone (although we have to provide it with private information under threat of punishment), but moreover, people are usually indignant when they find out that someone is sabotaging the census or does not want the state to manage their health records.

In the case of democracy, on the other hand, there is a society-wide belief that the will of the majority creates the moral right to legislatively decide on the freedom, property (or, in extreme cases, lives) of the minority; the strange thing is that it only applies to the majority within a given state. A worldwide vote on redistribution or other laws would certainly provoke outrage and sharp rejection; and it probably wouldn't be accepted any better if a significantly smaller group than the state (town, village, family or random group of people) voted to force anyone to do anything. But when the state does the same, it is usually enough to justify that when the majority has decided, the minority should obey. However, if we were to take this argument seriously, we could not apply it only to elections, but not to any other situation; here too, unfortunately, we apply completely different standards to certain institutions than to others.

Similar examples can be found innumerable today; however, I see the catch in the fact that the more a person is burdened by statism, the more he is unable to see in them what they are supposed to point to. I would therefore like to help myself with historical examples, which have the advantage that we are able to look at them from a distance. For millennia, people believed that their rulers were something more than themselves; whether directly gods, chosen by God's will, or at least of noble blood (descendants of heroes, sometimes supernatural, i.e. a "better race", which was to be manifested in physical and psychological attributes). However, our ancestors were no fools, nor did they need modern technology to disprove these theories through simple observation; yet it took thousands of years for us as humanity to do so – simply because re-examining one's beliefs can be painful, it requires emotional maturity, courage and humility.

As a result of another multi-thousand-year-old paradigm, people believed that they could own each other (and subsequently their children) as spoils of war, for example. Today we reject slavery; however, this state has only lasted a few centuries (a fraction of the time most cultures have practiced it), so we can learn a lot from the surviving arguments of its advocates, who at one time overwhelmingly prevailed against the few fools among the abolitionist ranks standing in opposition. The slaveholders' defense reminded me of something upon closer examination; let's take a closer look at it:

• "Slavery has been in operation throughout the world since time immemorial; if there were a better arrangement, it would have prevailed long ago." Perhaps every publicly active anarchist is tired of hearing that if the state were so bad, it would have been replaced by anarchy long ago.

• "The negro needs a master; for he cannot take care of himself." Isn't there a general societal consensus that people need government (even those who don't want it) because without it they wouldn't be able to take care of themselves?

• "But who would pick cotton without slaves? There would be an economic collapse." How many people believe that without legislative regulation our economy would collapse?

• "Without masters, slaves would kill each other - and so would we!" The fear of survival tends to be one of the strongest; and therefore the need for the state is also defended by fears of murder.

• "In some parts of the world free people live worse than slaves in our country." The existence of poor countries with little respect for laws is sometimes seen as an argument against anarchy.

• "Let's be realistic - we're not going to abolish slavery anyway, so let's at least fight for better conditions for slaves." Even a number of libertarians describe the efforts of anarchists as utopian and call on them to promote freedom in a democratic process.

• "A world without slavers is nothing but pure utopia; the idea is nice, but it cannot work in practice." This statement doesn't even contain any argument, but I come across it about once a week - it just mentions the state instead of the slavers. I find it interesting that people today defend the state with very similar claims that they used to justify slavery hundreds of years ago. I attribute this not only to the fact that both of these institutions are based on the premise that obedience of a certain group of people to another group is socially beneficial (even if the specific parameters are diametrically different), but also to the fact that they are based on the generally accepted paradigms of the given time rather than on logic - the last mentioned (dis)argument also corresponds to this. The same theses can thus make sense in one cultural and civilizational framework, while appearing absurd in another; this is also why I believe that one day our descendants will look at the state in the same way as we look at slavery today (although I can't imagine that I would live to see it).

Although I expect that the various forms of statism are as old as states themselves, I believe that its current form is primarily determined by centralized state education. Whereas in the past people tended to deify their rulers (and were forced to obey them under threat of severe punishment), today these cults of personality have been replaced by the fetishization of institutions that we are taught throughout childhood to help and protect us.

name: 11. Crime
text:
If one person violates the rights of another, we typically call such behavior (in common parlance) a crime. The legal definition (at least the Czech one) is a bit more specific - it distinguishes crimes, misdemeanors, misdemeanors and delicts, but let's leave that aside for now; let's first focus on the (human) rights of the individual that may be violated by such an action. There are a number of ways they can be viewed; in our civilization for the last several hundred years, fortunately (at least declaratively), we have agreed on their universality, i.e. their validity for every human being without exception (however, practice lags behind this theoretical agreement in various ways - we discussed some examples in the chapter on adultism).

For the purposes of this book, I consider the most important division of rights into positive and negative. Positive rights - "to something" - mean claims to the various achievements of society; on the other hand, the negative ones - "from something" - consist in the fact that no one should interfere in our lives and limit our freedom. The former require some action (providing something) from other people, while the latter require "inaction" (not interfering). For a better understanding, let's look at a few examples: According to the positive right to life, education or expression, someone must ensure our survival, teach us or give us space to express ourselves; similar negative rights then only prohibit murder, hindering access to knowledge, or censorship. If we hesitate in a specific case, to which category a certain right falls, it typically helps to imagine an individual isolated from society (for example, on a desert island) - then there is no one to violate his negative rights (which remain intact), but neither guarantees positive ones (they are meaningless at that moment); so we can find out whether the right we are talking about requires the active intervention of others or not.

At first glance, it might seem that positive rights bring - as opposed to negative - only advantages, as they not only protect us from those who would perhaps want to limit our freedom, but also provide us with other guarantees and security; however, upon closer reflection, we find that it has two very fundamental hooks. The first consists in the dependence of the possibilities of guaranteeing positive rights on the material conditions of the given company – in order to be able to claim any assets against it, it must have a sufficient amount of resources that it could provide to the applicant; negative rights, on the other hand, remain the same, so the societal dispute about the degree of redistribution also disappears. The second – far more serious – problem lies in the fact that granting a (positive) right to anyone in general necessarily means limiting someone's (negative) right. How is that possible? Well, for example, if we make health care "free" for everyone, someone has to pay for it; we will either leave it to the voluntary decision of the payers (but then it is not possible to guarantee the given service), or we will force them to do so, which, however, is an interference with their rights. Negative rights have the wonderful property that even if everyone were to make full use of them, there would be no collision; on the other hand, any positive legal claim inevitably disturbs this balance and creates a conflict - someone will be restricted in their freedom and (violently) forced to do something.

If we agree that violating the negative rights of any person is a crime against that person, then the enforcement of positive rights must also be. If someone voluntarily decides to help others, they are not entitled to such help - it occurs out of the good will of the helper; however, if we establish it by law, we necessarily create someone else's obligation to guarantee this right. So we replace voluntariness with an obligation, the fulfillment of which we demand from people under the threat of punishment from the position of (physical) force, which is undoubtedly an interference with their negative rights. Regardless of how fancy we call this process or what we use to justify its necessity, nothing changes the fact that if we perceive the violation of negative rights (that is, attacks on someone's physical integrity or other property rights) as a criminal act, the logical consequence is the criminality of positive rights as such.

For non-state entities, we typically understand this principle very well. Although most of us can perhaps more easily sympathize with a pickpocket in dire pecuniary need than with a rich thief, we consider the theft of both to be crimes which we may perhaps (considering the plight of life) understand, but do not regard as a legitimate means of livelihood; and even if the persons in question did not steal only for themselves, but left part of the "earnings" to others. Or, for example, if someone strongly disagreed with the way their neighbor lives, raises "his" children, treats his body or health, (doesn't) save for his old age, etc., we would consider violent interference in his life a crime (if the person in question did not abuse children or do something similarly serious). Unfortunately, even here, in the minds of the vast majority of people, there is an exception for the state; not only do they not consider his threats to those who do not live according to his agenda (embodied in the legislation) to be criminal, but they also consider such actions (so many in the state's submission) to be desirable and entirely correct.

For about fifteen years, I have been publicly drawing attention to this different approach to the state and other entities, while closely monitoring the reactions of readers, listeners and viewers. They often explain to me that and why their perception is based on logical foundations, not on emotions instilled by state propaganda. Almost without exception, they refer to at least one of two reasons - the "free" services of the state or the will of the majority. However, when I ask if they would change their view of crimes committed by a non-state organization that would start providing something (perhaps on a large scale) "free for all" and allow a democratic vote on its operation (in the case of multinational corporations, perhaps more customers than small states have citizens), the answer is always negative; from this, in my opinion, it follows that these are not real reasons (if they were, they would also apply to non-state entities), but rather a kind of rationalization of a deeply rooted belief (not unlike when people excuse certain crimes because, according to them, they happen by God's will).

Another consequence of such thinking is that even defense against the state is considered a crime; and even when we consider completely identical behavior to be legitimate towards anyone else. If an armed assailant breaks into our home in the middle of the night, we can shoot him in self-defense without being considered a criminal; but not in the case of an on-duty police officer - by knowingly shooting him, we become criminals under the law, even if the state makes a mistake and sends an emergency unit to another house by mistake (which, unfortunately, sometimes happens). If an organization collects our personal information and we do not provide it to them, we protect our privacy; however, let's try to do the same in the census - we risk a fine. And if we don't pay it? We immediately "robbed" the state, which has the "right" to enforce it (by force); but let's try to imagine that the same fine will be unilaterally imposed by another entity for not completing the questionnaire it sent us. Unfortunately, similar examples can be found innumerable; the state not only constantly commits legalized crimes, but also criminalizes those who try to resist it.

A special category of illegal behavior consists of so-called "crimes" without a victim. These are actions that are illegal, but do not interfere with anyone's autonomy, so they do not harm anyone who has not given their consent. Examples can be verbal crimes, failure to enroll a child in school, handling of psychoactive substances, assisted suicide, some consensual sexual activities, non-compliance with reporting obligations, desecration of state symbols, gathering of people without a permit, non-compliance with certain construction, hygiene, road or health standards, crossing the state border without a permit, illegal weapons, mutually voluntary pimping, illegal work or in violation of the Labor Code, over-limit cash operations, business without a license, tax evasion and many others. These are all activities that all parties concerned can agree to, yet the state still chooses to interfere and punish people for wanting to live their lives their way.

name: 12. Anarchy
text:
There are people living among us for whom crime means a violation of the (negative) rights of the individual, so that it always has a victim - without it, it cannot be a crime. They do not make exceptions to the "live and let live" rule; and not even for the state, which for them - since they are not statists - is nothing more than a powerful mafia that has managed to legalize itself. These people are called anarchists. Although the author of the earliest known surviving recorded anarchist ideas was the Taoist philosopher Lao-tzu (about two and a half thousand years ago), I assume that the first anarchist was born into the world around the same time as the first ruler. It is natural for some individuals to rule, to listen to others, and to live their own lives for others - while the first two groups more or less agree on the order of the world, at least in rough outlines (although they may differ in their opinion on who should lead others), while the third rejects their concept.

For most people, the word anarchy is essentially a derogatory term for chaos. Anarchists reject such vulgarization of this term, based on its etymology, namely the Greek anarchos, composed of the prefix an- (without) and the root archos (ruler); anarchy therefore does not mean the absence of rules, but of rulers (and states). After all, probably everyone has seen the most famous anarchist symbol - the A in a circle; however, few people know that the circle is actually the letter O, which stands for the word order, which is why the whole pictogram symbolizes that anarchy means (spontaneous decentralized) order of things, not chaos. Although people against anarchy typically argue for the need for rules, perhaps none of the countless anarchists I know dispute this need. Rejecting all rules as such represents a diametrically different attitude than not submitting to their unilateral dictate from above.

Anarchism can be seen from a certain point of view as "global respect"; that is, not only to close or at least familiar people, but to all individuals and their subjective preferences, needs, attitudes and values - including those whose existence we have no idea about. However, respect certainly does not mean that anarchists should perhaps agree with everyone and share their opinions (very often we are not even able to do this among ourselves); it is about accepting one's own and others' fallibility and recognizing that we are (despite differences in possibilities and abilities) equal as human beings - and therefore it does not make sense to elevate ourselves above anyone or humiliate ourselves in front of anyone, because by doing so we create at most a temporary illusion of inequality. Writing these lines about anarchism in general is not easy for me, because often after formulating a sentence, one of my anarchist friends or colleagues comes to mind, for whom my statements do not actually apply; this shows how diverse anarchism is as a school of thought and a belief in life.

The foundations of modern anarchism (without using the word) were laid by the philosopher William Godwin at the turn of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries; the first to call himself an anarchist was the socialist Pierre-Joseph Proudhon almost half a century later; he was followed by the individualist Max Stirner and the revolutionary Mikhail Alexandrovich Bakunin. It can be said that at that time anarchism was divided into two basic currents – individualist (emphasizing the freedom of the individual) and collectivist (perceiving man primarily as a social creature in the context of society). The work of the scholar Stirner was mainly followed by other thinkers, in the twentieth century, for example, Murray Newton Rothbard, the spiritual father of anarcho-capitalism; in the footsteps of the fighter Bakunin (the greatest opponent and critic of Karl Marx in the First International), rather agitators and fearless activists followed, for example, the anarchist prince Petr Alexeyevich Kropotkin, (one of) the founder(s) of the anarcho-communist movement and the author of the sentence: "One courageous act will do more work than a thousand pamphlets." This only shows that among anarchists we can find people of all kinds - peaceful intellectuals as well as militant revolutionaries.

In the last two centuries, up to a few dozens of different anarchist trends or offshoots have emerged; they more or less overlap, although sometimes they are quite distant from each other - although I have been intensively devoted to anarchism for about half of my life and personally know hundreds of its followers, the diversity of their views continues to fascinate me. We will probably only agree that we do not want to be ruled; but not entirely on what all can fall under such a government. Individualist anarchists tend to be voluntarists at the same time – that is, advocates that all human interactions should be voluntary, while their collectivist counterparts often have a problem with all hierarchies (even voluntary ones). Not that there aren't voluntarists among collectivist anarchists, or that none of the individualists can point to the dangers of hierarchies (as I do, for example). Anarcho-capitalists equate anarchy with capitalism, while (not only) anarcho-communists see them as opposites. There is no consensus (across the entire movement) on the legitimacy (or even the meaningfulness) of using direct violence (which creates great contradictions, especially among collectivists) or participation in political struggle in democracy (this is again a topic in the camp of individualists). I will elaborate on my positions on these issues in later chapters; here it is important for me to mention that as much as I respect the opinions of (not only) other anarchists, and hold many of them in high esteem, I certainly cannot speak for anyone but myself.

Although some anarchists reject capitalism, others socialism, and others, for example, patriarchy, perhaps all without exception do not recognize the legitimacy of the state; it unites us and at the same time distinguishes us from virtually all other people. Few people have a neutral attitude towards the state; while some consider it desirable and correct, or at least fundamentally necessary for the peaceful functioning of a developed society, others see the exact opposite in it – that is, a violent criminal organization. Anarchist Jeffrey Albert Tucker once posed a rhetorical question to which he answered himself: "Why anarchy? Because anything less would be uncivilized." I think he deliberately used words that express the emotions that statists often feel towards anarchy - they see it as something inferior, backward, crude, or even at odds with humanity itself - they fear it. On the other hand, it would not be fair to pretend that many anarchists from the state do not have a similar fear; especially those of us who, in (direct or indirect) connection with our attitudes and values, were summoned, beaten, not to mention got to know the cells of preliminary detention or prison from the inside.

Not only do these mutual concerns greatly complicate any substantive dialogue between the two sides; they especially enter into all the considerations we carry out on this topic. A person is brought up to be a statist; he typically becomes an anarchist of his own volition. However, as I could observe myself and large tens or small hundreds of other people, such a paradigm shift does not only require information and logical arguments; above all, we need the willingness to question everything we believed in, what we lived in, what we relied on and what may have formed a non-negligible part of our life's certainties - then our world may never seem the same again. Not to mention that as a result of such a transformation, we may be forced to face a lot of mistakes, or even mistakes, the consequences of which could harm not only us, but also other people. At the same time, we don't have to be a police officer from the anti-drug unit, who realizes years later that he didn't help and protect, but hurt and harm, which he decides to change and start doing something beneficial (I actually met such a person, this is the real story of Neil Woods), so that we can still feel sad about some actions in our past. All of this, understandably, evokes emotions in us that make it difficult to take the distance so necessary to reassess deeply rooted attitudes (whatever they may be).

If you feel that you are accessible and open to thinking about a stateless society, but you simply cannot imagine it, I dare you to recommend my book Anarchocapitalism. In it, chapter by chapter, I deal with individual state-managed or (re)regulated industries and show how and why they would function more efficiently without central management, but above all in accordance with ethics based on respect and voluntariness. If you can imagine such a society or don't even need to know what it looks like to dismiss the state as a criminal organization, please continue reading; on the following pages, I will first describe the paths that, in my opinion, do not lead to anarchy - although this may not be obvious at first glance - and I will explain why, then with these conclusions in mind, I will present a way in which we can effectively achieve the maximum possible degree of freedom, first in general, then also on specific examples with an emphasis on the possibilities of implementation in the lives of each of us.

name: 13. Revolution
text:
In the ranks of anarchists, we find many revolutionaries (especially if we look into the past) - often even convinced that real change in society cannot be achieved without a violent revolution. Therefore, it is not surprising that many people associate the anarchist movement with the pursuit of revolution or civil war, although in reality there is definitely no general agreement on the use of such means. Personally, I not only do not believe in this path, I even consider it strongly counterproductive; and not only to achieve anarchy as a target state, but also to increase the degree of freedom. Since one can also find rare historical examples of revolutions leading to (at least in the short term) a freer society, I cannot completely rule out this possibility. However, I am convinced that violent coups not only have a small chance of success (which, unfortunately, history confirms), but above all, in most cases, they fundamentally harm freedom (no matter how they turn out). In this chapter, I would like to show that armed coups do not end in tyranny by chance, but are more or less destined for it (they can turn out well only by a lucky coincidence, and probably only temporarily).

To begin with, let's imagine a hypothetical scenario in which I somehow became the unlimited ruler of the state - the army and the police would obey me, I could give them any orders. Of course, such a thing is not realistic - and I wouldn't give a damn about it - but I want to illustrate that even with such force I cannot transform a state society into an anarchist one, if the people do not want it. Almost everyone today lives in the belief that the state needs; therefore, if I dissolved it from a position of strength, almost everyone would try to restore such an organization again (but probably without me). If, in response, I were to use my power to prevent them from doing so by force (or at least intimidate them by such a threat), I would become the state myself. For they have a right to organize themselves as they please, so long as they do not attack me, which they probably will not do so long as I am stronger; but when I cease to be, he conquers me. Perhaps I can prevent this by using my power to subdue them first; but in no case will the result be free anarchy—either they rule me or I rule them—until there is a wider social demand for it.

One hundred and fifty years ago, the First International fell apart as a result of the conflict between anarchists and Marxists (they then founded the Second International, in which the anarchists were replaced by social democrats). The original cause of the split can be considered Marx's plan to control the state by the working class and use it to liquidate the bourgeoisie, which was supposed to lead to a classless society; Bakunin strongly objected that the result would be the creation of other classes, on the contrary – the leaders of the proletariat would become what they had originally fought against, which unfortunately history proved him to be right (George Orwell describes it illustratively in Animal Farm). Interestingly, neither Bakunin himself nor many of his followers (to this day) see the analogy between a violent revolution in the name of anarchism and the seizure of the state by Marxist means - while both rely on the widespread assertion of their opinion (whatever) by force against opponents through an action that, if successful, will give a group of (probably angry and determined) people power over others who they see as their oppressors so strongly, that they were willing to risk their lives to get rid of them. And just as Bakunin (quite rightly) objected to Marx that after the seizure of the state there will be a corruption of power and the emergence of a new ruling class, I would like to warn Bakunin's revolutionary successors that the seized power will probably remain like Sauron's ring during the revolution and corrupt its bearers.

However, even if we did not directly choose anarchy as our goal, but were content with any movement towards freedom, I am convinced that even then revolution would not represent a very promising path. Although we cannot completely rule out this possibility (such examples can rarely be found in history), on the one hand it would require a rather unfree society in the initial state, because even after a potential civil war miracles cannot be expected; above all, no one can reliably predict such success (let alone design it in practice), so it happens more or less by chance. For example, in 1991, after the revolution in Somalia, there was a relative increase in the degree of freedom (but it was so low before that hardly anyone would want to live there even after the improvement). However, this was only due to a stalemate between the warring factions, none of which could gain dominance over the others, which they all tried to do; rather than a pre-planned outcome, it was therefore a failure of the plans of all involved.

To better explain why I don't believe in revolution, let's look at the different possibilities of how it might turn out for someone trying to achieve freedom. The first risk lies in the suppression of the coup itself; everyone is probably counting on that. However, I am at least as worried about what will happen in the event of a successful coup. This is related to the second danger, which is the hijacking of the revolution; because it creates an opportunity for power grabs by people who can pretend to be freedom fighters, even though they may have just wasted a chance to rule or otherwise improve themselves. I see the third threat in the revolutionaries' inability to implement their (perhaps initially good) intentions in practice. After all, leading society in a certain direction requires different qualities than the ability to (perhaps matter-of-factly) criticize and subsequently depose the previous government. I perceive the fourth – perhaps the most insidious – pitfall in the inner change of those who go through something as merciless as a civil war. Their dark sides are likely to rise to the surface, as a result of which they may thirst for revenge rather than liberation. I think it is important to emphasize that at each of these obstacles the road to freedom can completely fail (and make the situation worse); on the contrary, even conquering everyone is not a guarantee of a freer society in the long term.

A necessary condition of any revolution is at least two strong opposing factions; otherwise there is either no one to overthrow, or no one to do it. Their intense conflict (however it turns out) will create a lot of angry, desperate, hurt and scared people; moreover, many of them will perceive the recent events as a wrong against themselves or their loved ones. It is hard to imagine a worse starting point for building a free society; after all, even in relatively calm times, we can observe individuals who want to exchange (not only their) freedom for (the illusion of) security out of fear. In the event of a successful coup, the victors may have (sometimes justified) fears of a counter-revolution; their attention is thus often directed more towards (often paranoid) defense against (perceived or real) enemies than towards the creation of what they perhaps once dreamed of - first of all, it is necessary to ensure safety from omnipresent threats - and thus short-term unfreedoms become long-term, temporary ones become permanent...

In addition, the revolution leads to the thinking style that if we do something now, good will win over evil, so it will be over and we will be (forever) well. I find a similar way of thinking (not only in this area) destructive; people often feel that something needs to be done once, forgetting that it is a long-term process. Just as we don't secure a healthy, functional relationship by choosing "the right one" or a fulfilling career by succeeding in an interview—both depend primarily on subsequent work—nor does freedom come from overthrowing an oppressor. It can be the first step in a long journey, but if we focus too much on it and exhaust ourselves with it, we reduce the chance of success - much like some poor people who quickly become poor again after winning the lottery because they get a false sense that they are "done" and don't need to keep trying. Throughout my life, I have been constantly reinforcing the belief that basically everything that is worth something lies in the everyday; only exceptionally in great deeds and perhaps never in gestures. With only a tiny bit of simplification, I dare to say that if society does not desire freedom, no revolution will change it; and conversely, if people's thinking is free, no coordinated coup is needed to liberate them - the state of the environment in which they live will adapt itself over time to their setting, because it originates from it.

Sometimes, looking back, it can seem that the coup liberated some nations - the revolutionaries managed to win, not lose their ideals and then implement them; however, I believe that in order for this to happen, the given society must have been inclined to freedom before. A king, communism, nazism can be imposed on the people, and they can even be forced to vote in democratic elections; however, they must want freedom, no one can dictate it to them from above - even if that happened, they wouldn't know what to do with it anyway. On the contrary, free-spirited individuals are difficult to control; they don't have to plot a coup in order to help each other and create a non-negligible force in society that refuses to obey (I will elaborate on exactly what this means in the following chapters). That's why I believe that the revolution has a chance to bring freedom basically only where it would otherwise happen through gradual development (even if a little later); however, if the coup plotters do not hit the right window of opportunity, they very easily achieve the opposite. Civil war may indeed replace a despotic ruler with a better one; absolutely every war, however, with probability bordering on certainty, will change the whole society for the worse, which is difficult to compensate for by the most self-enlightened monarch.

When I talk about revolution, I mean mainly a violent (or threat of violence) coup leading to a change of regime (or at least government); in exceptional cases, this happens essentially non-violently, which some readers certainly experienced in 1989, when the coup d'état also led to a jump in the degree of freedom in the then Czechoslovakia. I believe that the bloodier and more brutal the rebellion develops, the more likely it will eventually lead to unfreedom. On the contrary, the more peaceful and gradual the change takes place, the higher the chance it will give us to live freely in the long term - after all, even the aforementioned Velvet Revolution brought sudden liberation, but it was followed by a gradual erosion of freedom that continues to this day, which I explain by the fact that society was simply not ready for such a thing (even if it perceived it much better than the previous regime). I believe that pushing change "to power" from above generally works worse in the long term than starting with yourself and looking for your own freedom in everyday life; we will deal with this in detail in the very next chapter.

name: 14. Politics
text:
"So if you reject the revolution, you have only one way to get freedom - you have to change the laws democratically." I hear this phrase sometimes; and I admit that it sounded logical to me for a long time - it makes sense to anyone who internally agrees with the rules of the democratic regime to which we have been led since childhood. It took me most of my life to recognize the false dilemma in her. I'm writing this book with the hope that maybe thanks to it you'll discover it before I do. So what does it consist of? The above statement contains an unspoken assumption that laws are relevant until they are repealed or changed by someone – whether the current parliament, or a new ruler installed by a revolution, or some legislative body. Such thinking is characteristic of obedient people, for whom the legislation given by the state is an integral and important part of life; and if it is bad, they feel the need to modify it, to improve it. However, if we leave this paradigm, we will also see another possibility: Laws can be ignored throughout society so massively that not only they, but also the entire state apparatus become completely irrelevant; then neither a revolution nor a vote in parliament is needed. Already in the next chapter you can read how exactly I imagine it; for now, I just want to point out that if the state becomes insignificant, it is not necessary to decide whether to reform it by open violence or by political means.

Feminist Audre Lorde titled one of her critiques of patriarchy with the phrase: "The master's tools will never dismantle the master's house." I have taken the liberty of borrowing this aphorism because I believe that much more can be illustrated by it. For when I relate it to the topic of social freedom and translate it into the language of Austrian economics, it tells us that just as central planning fails in everything from the production of toilet paper to the education system, there is no reason why it should not similarly fail in shrinking the state. I find it interesting how many libertarians, on the one hand, understand that and why no politician can effectively manage society "from above" (even in quite trivial matters), but on the other hand, believe in the possibility of a targeted and planned reform of an extremely complex state apparatus towards freedom. But isn't this belief as foolish as when socialists elect their representative with the belief that he can actually redistribute the money of the rich in such a way as to actually help the poor and not harm the economy?

Let's imagine an honest and capable person who really cares about freedom; let's say he gets other such people together, forms a political party with the goal of actually limiting state power, and devotes his energies to winning the favor of voters. What will happen? Most likely (in our current civilizational context) their party will not be given a mandate to influence anything significant; most likely, he will not even cross the electoral threshold – i.e. he will not get the minimum number of votes (typically five percent) needed to enter a legislative body (perhaps parliament). Most people currently have other priorities than principled freedom; not that they actively desire unfreedom, but rather it is not an issue for them, so they can be better lured by promises of various achievements and services of the state (for which, unfortunately, they unwittingly pay with freedom). What then is left for our free-thinking politicians? They have the option of accepting failure and losing one election after another; at the same time, they can spread awareness and try to create a demand for freedom, however, they could also do this as a non-political organization - probably even more effectively, because a political party that is unsuccessful in elections in the long term demotivates not only its own members, but also potential (not only financial) supporters.

If our honest and capable party officials remain faithful to their ideals despite electoral failures, nothing really happens together; at most, their energy could be used more effectively in terms of achieving freedom. The catch is that political marketing will sooner or later come into play in getting votes; it will become apparent that certain topics cannot be communicated to voters too radically, so the rhetoric will be softened. This doesn't matter at first - it's not necessary to lie, it's enough just not to say certain things, while rewording others a bit. If this leads to the expected results, two other things are likely to happen: First, one can count on greater or lesser impacts on existing party members; each of us is influenced by everything he says, that is, the more a party member is involved in political work, the more gradually his thinking will at least to some extent adapt to how he presents himself on the outside. Secondly, this party also attracts (as applicants for membership) people for whom its original ideals are unacceptable (however, they have ceased to be communicated directly), while they accept them in a milder form (albeit with certain reservations); the recruitment of such members logically means a departure from freedom.

I was personally a close witness of the birth, rise and fall of a party that at the very beginning had freedom as the highest value. In the first years after its establishment, its members publicly proposed, for example, the abolition of compulsory schooling or the decriminalization of all drugs. The first electoral failures were followed by endless internal party debates about the fact that this is not the way to communicate with voters; and so criticism of compulsory schooling turned into criticism of only pre-school, the decriminalization of all drugs narrowed down to just marijuana, and other topics turned out similarly. The election victory did come; and the membership grew like out of water - both pragmatists who sensed a chance to assert themselves in politics, but also people who, according to their words, wanted freedom, but only from here to there. With them, calls for personal responsibility in providing for old age turned into campaign promises to increase pensions during the decade, and party leaders began to openly oppose even the legalization of marijuana. When the pre-election polls did not give them a chance to cross the five percent threshold, they did not hesitate to sign up for the candidates of other parties calling for the restriction of freedom of expression, the nationalization of businesses, the setting of prices by law or the nationalization of the property of the rich. I don't see this development as an unfortunate coincidence or human failure; in my opinion, this is a logical consequence of the effort to assert freedom through political means in a society that does not (yet) care about it.

The stronger the societal demand for freedom, the more we will not need politicians to achieve it; people will go after it on their own without a central plan—even in spite of bad laws they can bend, circumvent, covertly break, or openly defy. The more free-thinking individuals around us, the easier it will be to live our own way even where the state tries to limit our lives. Illegal behavior does not have to be condemned by society - on the contrary, in the case of "crimes" without a victim, there may be understanding or even support for it. Not to mention that the societal demand will make the most prominent libertarians the biggest populists among contemporary legislators; it will not be about their real inner convictions, but they can still override restrictive legislation. Society does not follow politicians; that politicians follow society. If we want to live freely, we need to start with ourselves and set an example for others; politicians will adapt - just as those from the previous paragraph adapted to the demand for a strong state.

Internally free people do not need a leader; the unfree ones do - and they always find him. Therefore, I believe that "free politicians" in the democratic world must sooner or later pay with their souls (or accept failure): Either they will remain true to their ideals and thus not achieve anything, or they will make compromises - for voters, coalition partners, the opposition, their own party. How long can you live in something like that without it starting to change you from the inside? Do you have any idea how many years you can successfully operate in a win-win environment without losing yourself? I don't; and I'm not even going to try because if that happens I won't care anymore - I won't have the motivation to change. Unfortunately, I've watched that process more times than I'd like with my acquaintances (libertarians) who entered politics over the years...

Politics is sometimes called the art of compromise. But what is the compromise between the greater and lesser evil? Truth and lies? Freedom and unfreedom?

Even if a politician succeeds in winning votes, overcoming his own demons, and dealing with his party's drift away from freedom, he will run into another obstacle—namely, the cumbersome nature of legislative change. The laws are hellishly complex, they follow each other and their adjustments require a high degree of expertise. Basically, all fundamental reforms are additionally complicated by civil servants accustomed to certain processes that they do not want to give up; dealing with them requires a style of communication (and thinking) typically different from that of free-thinking individuals. Even if a politician learns to walk in all this, it will take a long time; however, this is limited by the length of the electoral term. How much can be done during it? Even experienced government matadors often have trouble getting their changes through; and they usually do not deviate too much from the captured standards. Real reforms, i.e. a real reduction of the state, which would be at least somewhat reflected in our lives, would probably require several consecutive election periods. How likely do you think it is that someone would retain his mandate during that time without the opposition discrediting his work, the tangible results of which are likely to be seen over a longer time horizon? Is it even possible to significantly reduce the state in our society and at the same time maintain popularity?

I am not saying that no improvement can ever be achieved by political means; after all, I welcome any removal of the restrictive law, and moreover I admit that one can find (mainly historical) examples of politicians who did something like this systematically (although these are rare exceptions). However, I believe that in the long run, all the energy spent on this (including their teams, collaborators, partisans and voters - i.e. tens to hundreds of millions of hours per election period in one country) would help freedom more if they invested it decentralized and did not attempt central planning. A successful politician, on principle, influences people to give him their votes; but doesn't this lead to a sense of transfer of responsibility from the voters to the state? Doesn't that reinforce in them the feeling that they need to be led? And isn't the need for leadership at the root of the whole problem with lack of freedom?

name: 15. Liberation
text:
In the previous chapters, I gradually rejected the (violent) revolution and the political path as dysfunctional means to expand freedom. So what is my recourse? Anarchoagorism – a market anarchist strategy to achieve freedom. The anarchist Samuel Edward Konkin III came up with it for the first time in 1983. (he often used the abbreviation SEK3 instead of the name) in his work The New Libertarian Manifesto. In it, he rejects participation in elections and politics in general (he sharply criticizes the American political party Libertarian Party), while highlighting the gray economy, ignoring the state and the cooperation of free individuals in non-state markets - the so-called agoras. Before I elaborate on these ideas further, I would like to point out two things to the reader: First, although SEK3 writes about agorism and I write about anarchoagorism, these are synonyms; I use the term anarchoagorism both because I got to know it earlier, but also because it seems more accurate. Secondly, after reading the New Libertarian Manifesto, it may seem to some people at first glance that it is about something else (perhaps because in it you can read about the revolution and in general it is written more "offensively" than this book) - however, I believe that the difference lies in the different use of language, because the attentive reader will find in the manifesto sharp words, but also clear calls not to initiate violence (including preventive strikes) and the like.

Anarchoagorism is not a fight against the state; it is about the creation of parallel structures (agoras) that fulfill a variety of functions - including those on which the state usurps a monopoly. Agoras were gathering places (marketplaces) in the middle of ancient cities where public life took place; it was not only about trade, but also about (philosophical and other) debates and other interpersonal (conciliatory and conflictual) interactions. In a figurative sense, it is a free (not only physical) space, where the arrangement of things does not arise from the orders of authorities, but from voluntary relationships and spontaneous order; it logically follows that the state's power is limited in such an environment. Rather than a place, the Agora can be thought of as a community of people; they can communicate through any channels (in person, by correspondence, online or in any other way), but their interactions are mutually voluntary. Agora can provide various services to its members (and actually also non-members or other agoras) and perform functions that are currently provided by the state (albeit involuntarily).

It is important to realize that state power always comes from the actions of specific people; therefore, by associating individuals who do not recognize any ruler (man or institution), islands of freedom can be created even in an otherwise relatively unfree society. I myself participate in several agoras; in some only occasionally, I practically live in two and consider them my family. Each of them is completely different (they differ in the subject of interest, the number of members, the method of communication and other parameters), however, the regulations of external authorities (such as the state) fall into all of them only "from the outside", because their members do not aimlessly enforce them within the community; not that we never follow them (sometimes together we evaluate the risks as too high), but we perceive them as obstacles to functioning, not as something that we should "properly" follow.
