This also results in considerable freedom of action within the agora; the power of external authorities is shielded to a great extent by the fact that its members solve their disputes and problems internally (in extreme cases, even by leaving), not by appealing to these authorities (or even involving them in internal affairs).

There is no need to imagine anything mysterious or unattainable under the term agora; with a certain degree of anarchist thinking, a family or a group of friends can easily become her, without them even being aware of it. I know agoras that someone founded directly with the aim of creating a parallel non-state structure, but also a lot of those whose creation did not even have such an idea; one of them is even the entire (private) school Jezek without a cage, where I work. You can read more about it and other specific examples in the Practice chapter, where I describe individual projects that bring more freedom to our world. For now, however, it will suffice to see agoras as communities of people respecting the mutual voluntariness of their interactions and not recognizing the legitimacy of interventions by self-appointed authorities from the outside (which does not mean that they cannot sometimes submit to them if they find the consequences of disobedience too severe).

Anarchoagorism consists not only in practical functioning within parallel structures, but also in the spread of anarchist (and economic) theories. Actors of the gray economy are typically perceived by society more or less negatively, which is then also transferred to how the persons in question view themselves; they hide not only out of fear of retribution, but also out of shame - over time, they accept the reactions of those around them as their own, so they begin to see themselves as outcasts. Not infrequently, they approach their activity in such a way that they earn something now so that they can make an "honest" living at some point in the future; they miss the fact that there is nothing dishonest about not handing over protection money, even if we call it taxes - it is still a coercive payment under the threat of violence. Since I have been spreading this view to the world for almost twenty years, I have had the opportunity many times to observe the relief of someone who considered himself a bad person, but by accepting an anarchist perception of the world, he came to the fact that he does not do anything morally wrong, even though society has convinced him of this since childhood; and the theories of the Austrian economic school, in turn, show him that his illegal activity does not even reduce anyone's well-being - quite the contrary.

I consider participation in the gray economy one of the keys to freedom. Every penny we hand over to public budgets can be used to curtail our freedoms; but that is far from all - with every service provided outside the purview of state power, we show in practice that we do not need a central authority to manage our lives, because we are capable of doing it far better ourselves. Personally, I try to avoid all payments to the state, but also not to take anything from it, so as not to be dependent on it; I'm not able to fully do either one - I can't completely avoid taxation (especially indirect taxes), but I can't avoid using services in state-monopolized sectors (I use roads, for example). Still, I try to minimize both; by not giving what I don't have to, but above all I don't work for the state and I have never taken any money from it in my life, although I could. There are libertarians who, on the contrary, draw as much as possible from the state in order to weaken it. I understand their arguments, but I don't agree with this approach for two reasons: First, I have a strong emotional aversion to accepting hard-earned money from the time I can remember (if I were to do it myself, I wouldn't feel good about myself, even though it doesn't evoke those emotions in me when others do it); above all, however, I want to be as little dependent as possible on the central government (which is also why I will save for my pension all my life, so that I don't have to take state money even on my old knees).

I can often not only ignore public power, but also peacefully do my bit to paralyze it by bringing upon myself the resources with which it attacks me when I have the capacity to do so. An example can be a road (or any other) inspection that the state sends to me, even if I don't do anything to anyone (and even according to the law, everything is fine). I can make the course of this activity difficult and slow down (sometimes quite effectively, if I know the corresponding legislation), which will cause, on the one hand, that they cannot deal with someone else at the same time, but above all, I do not bow to the executors of state power. They are used to the devout approach of the controlled, as a result of which they generally allow themselves more; the more often they encounter resistance (perhaps even within the limits of all decency), the less they dare, and moreover, their work is not so attractive for individuals who wish to bully others from a position of power. The art of dealing with state authorities as equals (I'm not talking about being rude or condescending to them) also expands the horizons of our (primarily internal) freedom.

The goal of anarchoagorisism is the creation of parallel structures of sufficient relevance and strength so that the state would not necessarily disappear as an organization, but would not be able to continue to enforce its monopoly on violence against them; this would make his legislation irrelevant to part of society. Anarchoagorists would then not be bothered by the fact that statists want to continue living according to the laws of their rulers; their agoras would follow their own order independent of any government. Such a thing is probably presupposed by an armed populace willing to resist violence; but that doesn't mean the process can't happen peacefully—the establishment can choose not to attack and risk a bloody civil war if the anticipated backlash is too great. Nothing like this is imaginable today, but if a non-negligible part of society lives in accordance with anarcho-agorist principles, the state itself will begin to shrink and lose the power to exercise its power. However, we are certainly not that far today; however, we can already create islands of freedom where the power of external authorities can reach only to a limited extent.

How is anarcho-agorism related to anarcho-capitalism? I believe that both of these schools of thought have the same goal - a free, free market society; however, they differ in the approach to achieve this goal. While anarcho-agorists reject the political path, anarcho-capitalists do not reject it (but neither do they require it); that is, an anarcho-capitalist can be an anarcho-agorist at the same time (for example, I am both), but need not be. There are also anarcho-agorists who do not consider themselves anarcho-capitalists, as they see capitalism as corporate fascism rather than the free market. I personally consider anarchoagorism to be a "pure" version of anarcho-capitalism in the sense that its (non-political) means do not contradict the (non-political) end.

Before we get into disobedience in the next chapter, I'd like to warn about some counterproductive steps on the way to freedom. Please, let's not restrict the freedom of people who we think are doing something wrong; if they want to be led by someone and create (voluntary) hierarchies, let's not stop them (after all, everyone who needs guidance will eventually find one), even if it may seem dangerous to us - let's not strike preemptively. The better way, in my opinion, is to have a dialogue, especially as long as no one is (physically) attacking. Against a word with a word, against a sword (at most) with a sword. And even those words can be used peacefully (albeit clearly and steadfastly); calling people enemies of liberty typically does not make them friends.

name: 16. Disobedience
text:
I consider disobedience to be a necessary individual prerequisite for an individual to be able to embark on an anarcho-agorist path. I do not mean that if (as a result of upbringing, perhaps) we gravitate toward obedience, we cannot be anarchoagorists; however, I consider it important to be aware of my (dis)obedience and work with it. Since we live in a state-run society - and most people accept the state as at least necessary, or even deify it to some extent - this creates varying degrees of social pressure on anarchists; obedient or proud citizens may see us as a danger and a threat to their way of life. We can regularly perceive this most clearly during election periods, when non-voters often arouse greater opposition from voters than supporters of different political camps; they want us to conform—and it is our disobedience that allows us to not go with the crowd and live up to our values. But what exactly is (dis)obedience?

Developmental psychologist Lawrence Kohlberg defined six stages of moral development: fear of punishment; desire for reward; the need for relationships (typically manifesting as an effort to please others); blind obedience to laws (regardless of their content); acceptance of the social contract (it stands above laws that need to be changed or interpreted for the benefit of society) and finally living according to one's own ethical values and rules (despite any legislation). I agree with his conclusions, although I believe that they are (at least the first stages) relevant only in an environment where we work with punishments or rewards as basic tools of education, the goal of which is to make the child obedient; and obedience to parents or teachers easily turns into blind obedience to laws. After all, Kohlberg himself claims that only 15% of people over the age of 25 are in the fifth stage; while he describes the sixth as more "potential", because even those who think in it, typically cannot consistently align their opinions (and certainly not their actions) with it.

I have described four layers of (dis)obedience for the needs of anarchoagoris: The first layer is defined by the opinion that we should follow the legislation; this does not mean that the bearers of such beliefs cannot break the law (perhaps on purpose), they just do not generally consider it right. The second layer can be characterized by the sentence: "If you don't like the law, change it." We often hear this call especially from the advocates of democracy; their means of changing the world lie in politics or civic activism. The third layer leads to the realization that legislators are only human and their knowledge of our lives is necessarily very limited; therefore, it is difficult for them to design rules for us better than we ourselves. The logical way out is then conscious disobedience to legislation contrary to what we consider to be right; even so, we can sometimes choose to obey a bad law rather than face the consequences (just as individuals in the first layer can violate legal norms) – the layers of (dis)obedience describe a person's internal setting rather than their actions in each specific situation. So when we break the law, perhaps we help ourselves; but the bad legislation will not disappear from society. What about that? The answer lies in the fourth layer: After all, we can help others to break the law, show them the way, inspire them, share the necessary knowledge and skills. This is often illegal in itself, so risky; however, it can (if needed) be done more or less covertly (more on this in the Practice and Participation chapters).

Why do I consider trying to change laws to be a "lower" layer of (dis)obedience than breaking them? On the one hand, it is efficient - to change the legislation we need to spend a huge amount of energy, which can be more productively used not only to find ways to violate or circumvent it, but even to share this knowledge (disobedience can be scaled well in an environment where information spreads easily, which today's society fulfills very satisfactorily). But above all, I find it more ethical - I'd rather violate state law than my own moral integrity in trying to change it (in the previous chapter I explain why I think politics is a very dirty game); and I also don't want to contribute to the appearance of the legitimacy of legislation by seriously dealing with its creation, when I can rather reduce its legitimacy in the eyes of others by disrespecting it and thus create an environment where, rather than formal norms, we look at not restricting anyone's freedom, property and the like. I regard obedience as one of the most dangerous viruses of our civilization; and breaking the law are among the important ingredients of antivirus.

Here I will quote Howard Zinn again: "Civil disobedience is not our problem. Our problem is civil obedience. Our problem is that people around the world obeyed the orders of leaders; and because of that obedience, millions of people were killed." A huge mistake in assessing the harmfulness of obedience consists in taking into account its effects only in the good times of relatively peaceful societies, where it typically results in the "mere" imprisonment of individuals who have done no harm to anyone (and moreover there are units per thousand of the entire population). However, when we take into account the consequences in states of war and totalitarian regimes (which would never have a chance to exist without obedience), disobedience to the law ceases to appear to be such a dangerous alternative.

However, I consider it really important not to mistake disobedience for self-serving defiance or blind rebellion; it may help us in some phase of the life journey from obedience to disobedience, but in the end it is again just obedience in "disguise". If we start automatically doing the opposite of everything someone orders us to do, that person will still control our life; just in the opposite direction than he intends. However, if we want to live for ourselves and for ourselves, defiance of someone or something is not the answer. I know people who say they don't trust the government (whatever, I don't either), but in practice that means they tend to believe the opposite of everything the government says; but such an approach does not help much in the search for truth. When covid started and I knew practically nothing about it, I took a mask - voluntarily, even before the government order - I didn't mind wearing it, so I stuck with it; and for this he received sharp criticism from some fellow anarchists that I was a sheep blindly following the instructions of politicians. But taking off the mask just because it became mandatory would not be disobedience, but blind defiance or succumbing to collective pressure. I wore it (obviously not in the car, as the legislation required at the time) until it stopped making sense to me, which was a little earlier than the state allowed, but long after the absence of a veil was the sign of rebellion that some expected of me.

Although I have no problem not going with the crowd or living the way I want and need, I don't believe I'll ever get to the point where I'll be completely disobedient – that is, myself. I realize that it's easier to fall into the trap of blind defiance than direct obedience, and I try to work with that to discover more (albeit increasingly subtle) traces of obedience with each step toward my true self. Every year my son and I go to the Formula 1 Grand Prix, where the national anthem of the host country is always played before the race, so hundreds of thousands of people stand up at once, while I remain seated because I don't want to show respect to any country (I usually only get a few disapproving looks). However, just this year I was packing and about to get up by accident right as the anthem started – my first automatic reaction was to stay seated on purpose; only after a few moments did I realize that I didn't really want to rebel, but to sit or stand according to my own needs. Not that sitting or standing would matter in this case; however, I perceive it as a good example of something in me, which of course can also manifest itself in more important issues. Perhaps everyone understands that disobedience does not mean doing something just because someone tells us to; but it's not rebellion without a cause either - disobedience means being yourself.

The subtitle of this book is "Good people don't obey bad laws." But who are the good people? And which laws are the bad ones? What do I mean by that? As it follows from the previous chapters, I consider bad laws to be all that limit someone's negative (property) rights, or (external) freedom; this includes, but is not limited to, any legislation that guarantees anyone any positive rights (I explain this relationship in more detail in the Crime chapter). This is of course just my view; someone else might call completely different laws bad. And what if a good person is considered to be someone who wants to kill people in violation of the law? That too can happen; which does not mean that I agree with it - the purpose of this book is not to justify any aggression towards anyone, but rather to appeal for respect for anyone even where the law requires otherwise. With that subtitle, I'm trying to express my belief that although I realize that if people started following what they consider to be right instead of valid legislation, it would bring a lot of problems, but we would avoid much more suffering.

name: 17. Self-development
text:
I mentioned in the previous chapter that disobedience is being yourself. But what does that mean? From an early age, we are led to be good boys and girls, to achieve something in life, to achieve something (although no one really knows what and where), to surpass siblings, classmates or the children of neighbors or colleagues of our parents, and someone could be proud of us; under the weight of these demands, we pile on layers of false identities of imaginary people who manage everything, don't whine, don't have problems and always manage. The more effectively we can do this, the more we move away from our real "I", which may be sad or longing for something that is not compatible with the generally accepted idea of a successful individual in a given society; and so we cut off contact with this inappropriate "I", hiding it so deeply that we lose access to its needs. How then can we be disobedient? How can we be ourselves?

I find it crucial to understand the process of how this happened in the first place. From a very young age, we are expected to obey teachers, parents, but also various social norms - i.e. what is "done" or "not done" - behind which the needs of specific people may be hidden, but often they don't even have to be. I once rode a bus where a very young child, whose feet hadn't even reached the ground yet, started kicking the seat in front of him; when mom asked to leave it, he asked why. Her reaction surprised me: "Because it's not done. Do you see anyone else kicking the couch?" I can hardly imagine a worse answer. In addition to referring to an unspecified norm, rejecting otherness and calling for uniformity, it completely ignores any human needs - even I couldn't tell from that sentence what it was actually about. About the comfort of the passenger? Seat cleanliness? Did the baby's movement bother her? Was she afraid of falling to the ground? Maybe all together or something else; however, she did not try to impart any reason to the child, she destroys the need - she demanded blind obedience and conformity. Just to be clear, I am of course not advocating kicking seats; I am expressing myself purely to justify why not to do it.

Society hammers into us that wanting something for yourself is not as noble and noble as defending the interests of others; people (including parents) then often hide their wishes behind something higher and more general - they don't tell "their" children, for example, that they are afraid that others will judge them for their behavior, but they appeal to general decency; one's own feeling of being threatened by other people's emotions is often solved by trying to regulate the child's expressions; instead of the need for peace or quiet, they can talk to themselves, for example, about what good children (don't) do; they most often hide their inability or unwillingness to relinquish control as a concern for safety and the like. Children then adopt this way of communication - and especially thinking - as their own, as they constantly learn by imitation; they subsequently hide their real needs behind general norms. When they automate it enough, over time they become so distant from their needs that they stop being aware of them altogether; and eventually they will raise the next generation in a similar spirit.

If we want to break this chain, we need to start knowing ourselves. What do we really want? What are our wishes, goals, desires and dreams? And how to distinguish them from the expectations of the surroundings? First of all, we need to stop and take time for ourselves - stop solving work and daily tasks and focus only on what we have inside, how we feel, what we experience; try to be as honest as possible and do it repeatedly. How much time do we spend thinking about or choosing a vacation, a car, a job or a house? And isn't contact with our "self" even more important? Everyone is comfortable with something different - one prefers solitude in nature, another prefers to spend a few days staying in the dark, a third visits his therapist, coach or shaman, and a fourth may reach for psychedelics (which can be an effective way, but also quite risky - especially for inexperienced and insufficiently informed users). All of these (and many other paths) often lead to the realization that we are living life according to someone else's ideas instead of doing what fulfills us.

Sometimes, together with how we don't want to live, what we need also appears to us right away; however, if we are too disconnected from our self, only confusion can result. What then? Step by step to explore our inner self, change various aspects of our own life and see how it will be for us; only one thing is certain - it will hurt, because in order for it to work and for us to learn, we need to leave our comfort zone (in the discovery phase and when making life changes). It's not an easy journey, but it's definitely worth it; the reward lies not only in being happier, but also in self-knowledge and (inner) freedom, with other fascinating and fundamental consequences.

Through self-development, among other things, we come to know, believe and, above all, truly understand and accept that only we ourselves are responsible for our lives; we create it. The position of the creator is to realize that whatever we have within us is ultimately "ours"; and if we want change, its implementation is again up to us - we are the architects of our own happiness and unhappiness. The opposite of this attitude is the role of the victim. If we perceive ourselves as a victim, we look for culprits who are to blame for our suffering - parents, politicians, the rich, today's times, the state, capitalism, genetics, (ex)partners and the like. For example, an alcohol addict from the creator's perspective understands that no matter how he got into his condition, it is up to him how he (doesn't) deal with his addiction; on the other hand, in the victim setting, the same person will focus his attention from himself to others – the alcohol manufacturer, unregulated advertising, indifferent society or perhaps drunken friends. Each of us can look at the world through the lens of creator or victim; not every moment we are aware of this choice, but we can learn it (by persistent work on ourselves). The more time we spend as victims, the more prone we are to obedience - we believe that there is someone else who is responsible for our suffering - then a potential "leader" just needs to show us sufficiently believable culprits and offer a solution. These "authors of evil" can be Jews, bourgeois, kulaks, migrants, but also Russians, Germans, Americans or even state representatives. At the same time, it is not so important whether and to what extent the person in question really harms us; it depends on whether someone (typically a politician) can convince us to focus on fighting them instead of focusing on our own lives and values. Of course, the possibility cannot be ruled out that a conflict with members of one of the above-mentioned groups will occur within the framework of the protection and defense of one's own integrity; however, I consider it absolutely essential whether we only do what is necessary to protect ourselves, our loved ones (or other people), or whether we join a holy war in which we try to turn all our pain and anger against those we consider to be its masterminds (which, of course, we can playfully justify by saying that we are only defending ourselves), thus often becoming the very aggressors we set ourselves against.

How do we become immune to false saviors using us for their own interests? If we believe that someone other than ourselves can be responsible for our suffering or that someone other than us can ensure our happiness, we can be convinced of who (and against whom) we should (blindly) follow in order to solve our problems. On the contrary, the full realization that no one like that exists (or cannot exist in principle, because our life means only and only our responsibility), will allow us to resist all similar seductions, because in this context they do not even make sense. It follows that the stronger we desire in "righteous anger" to punish, for example, communists or Nazis for various atrocities committed in the name of their ideology, the easier we will succumb to the seductions of some modern-day Stalin or Hitler. The principle remains the same - it's always about the desire to fight someone or against someone instead of trying to live your own life.

Just as obedience manifests itself directly (following) and indirectly (defying at all costs), we can fall into the trap of not accepting responsibility for our lives, both as followers and as leaders. The more someone has a desire to lead people, bring order or justice in society and create a better world for others, the easier it is to fall into the illusion that something like this can be achieved "from above". It does not have to be just the state; even the anarchist "leaders of the revolution" fit the role of violent rulers (even if only temporarily). It is always an omission of the principle that everyone is responsible for his own life - just as it does not make sense for someone to be responsible for mine, it is no more meaningful for me to be responsible for the lives of others.

There are many books, seminars and various internet content devoted to the topic of self-development. In this chapter I have tried to summarize only the most important points for disobedience and anarchoagoris; unfortunately, this is only the tip of the iceberg (in fact, self-development is a complex path to mastering fear, and therefore to inner freedom), and moreover, just gliding over its surface. I imagine a lot of people might have had the following thoughts while reading the last few paragraphs:

• But sometimes I can really become someone's victim! Should I pretend it didn't happen?

• In a perfect world, everyone would be the architect of their own happiness; in practice no - some are lucky, others unlucky.

• What if a group of people is really hurting me? I'm not supposed to defend myself, am I?

• I can't wait for someone to attack me; I strike first!

• In order to live my life in peace, I must logically first defeat those who interfere with it.

• When someone harms people, he deserves a just punishment.

• In difficult times and crises, people simply need a leader.

• After all, the text excuses aggressors and predators - it blames the victims! The more strongly someone identifies with these theses, the more I expect that the time devoted to self-development could at least give them interesting topics to think about. Where to start? There are countless sources - an internet search engine or artificial intelligence will definitely give you a clue; I can personally recommend Marshall Rosenberg from foreign authors (his non-violent communication changed my life), Pavel Morice from Czech, or my own podcast Zrzka and Matfyzák. Everyone is comfortable with something different, there is no universally correct way; nevertheless, I consider it more or less impossible to live internally freely or to effectively achieve external freedom without knowing oneself (and on the contrary, ignorance of one's inner self often leads to disastrous or fatal consequences - a fighter for freedom can easily become an oppressor without noticing it).

name: 18. Sharing
text:
SEK3 ended the New Libertarian Manifesto by exclaiming, "Agora. Anarchy. Action!" Some slightly different words (albeit with similar meaning) came to me while writing this book: "Freedom; self-management; self-development; sharing." I have perhaps sufficiently described the meaning of the first three in previous chapters; I would like to dedicate this to sharing. Why is it so important? And what do I mean by that? This is both the voluntary transfer of material goods between people (in exchange for something, lending, but also gifting for a good feeling), as well as the spread of intangible goods, especially information. I believe that in the long run, all of this cumulatively leads to an increase in our degree of freedom - not necessarily each action, but collectively all of them together more often than not, so that we end up moving towards freedom just by interacting with each other in some way, which I find reassuring.

Let's start with material goods - voluntary exchange, loans and gifts (free market interactions do not necessarily have to be oriented towards financial gain) enable the division of labor, thereby increasing the efficiency of human behavior and thus the level of well-being. Without the ability to dispose of the fruits of others' labor, we would have no better chance of survival than a naked castaway on a desert island. By far the best tool for allocating resources among strangers is money and a price system; it is only thanks to him that we can effectively transfer information (and incentives) scattered throughout society, the complexity of which no human brain can even grasp, let alone plan sensibly (which, fortunately, is not even necessary). In smaller communities – agoras, families, tribes and the like – it is possible to meaningfully do without pricing. This (and millions of years of evolution in small groups) leads some people to mistakenly believe that even billions of individuals can organize in this way, which is not (and perhaps never will be) possible with the current state of knowledge, even assuming the best intentions of all involved; without money and a price system, we cannot effectively transmit information about human needs or the rarity of goods in such numbers.

But how are work efficiency and material well-being related to freedom? A careful reader of the first chapter of this book may remember that I strictly separated freedom from material possibilities (a person can be free without possessions and unfree in abundance); this might at first glance suggest that they are not related in any way. However, when we look at this issue in a broader context, we find out that individuals fighting for their bare lives or the lives of their loved ones will take up a weapon with the intention of robbing a neighbor of his resources more likely than those who have something to eat, where to sleep (ideally warm) and who are deciding where to fly to on summer vacation. Of course, this does not mean that materially secure people cannot make war; they just risk their entire existence less willingly compared to the situation where the survival of themselves or their family is at stake.

Living in material abundance gives us one more fundamental advantage – and that is free time; when we don't have to hunt for food in the forest (or toil in the field) from morning to evening, we have room for thinking and purposefully exploring the (internal and external) world. In the ancient past, it was necessary for the survival of our ancestors to accept as undeniable facts many statements simply because they were presented to them; they never had to think about and question them (because they used up practically all of their energy to make a living), which made them easier to control individuals, which rulers, churches, and various charlatans liked to use. Even in modern history, a similar strategy can be encountered, albeit on a shorter scale - the Nazis were able to control a large number of prisoners with a relatively small number of guards, among other things, by constantly assigning them something and keeping them busy, which was sometimes done only so that they could not stop, think about their situation and perhaps come up with some plan of resistance or escape. If we don't have time to think, we lose our freedom more easily; the more space we gain for reflection, the higher the chance we have of becoming more resistant to oppression.

I consider the dissemination of information to be at least as important as the sharing of material goods; with advancing technological progress, the transaction costs of data transmission are constantly decreasing - messengers, carrier pigeons, printing press, telegraph, telephone, radio, television, internet... As time goes on, we need fewer and fewer resources to learn something. Why was it necessary in the past to travel to a (many times far away and not always accessible to everyone) library (if a person could read at all, which even a few hundred years ago the vast majority of people could not), today it is enough to reach into your pocket for your phone and ask an internet search engine or artificial intelligence. In this way, all useful information, but also lies, slander, myths or half-truths can be spread more and more effectively; however, I believe that even if potentially harmful content spreads as quickly as needed content, in the end reducing the transaction costs of (all) communication will help freedom rather than harm it. Why do I think that?

Ludwig von Mises wrote: "The criterion of truth is that it works, even if no one is willing to admit it." He was pointing to the fact that certain principles and laws (such as physical or economic) apply regardless of whether people know or believe in them; their discovery and understanding then enables us to better orientate ourselves in the world (knowledge of physics can help, for example, in aviation or electronics, economic knowledge discourages us from, for example, central planning and the like). It follows that in the long term, individuals and communities living in the truth will be statistically more successful than those who profess delusions. Belief that truth prevails, therefore, does not have to be based on naive wishful thinking; evolution and game theory are also behind it - mystification is not a profitable strategy in the long run. But what does that say about freedom?

Thousands of years ago, rulers were able to convince their subjects that they were gods on earth; hundreds of years ago only that they rule by the will of God; decades ago at least that they need a fully centrally planned economy (but no longer references to religion); today, even this illusion is gradually disintegrating, although it still holds in some fields. The better access humanity has to information, the more difficult we are to be controlled by the mystification of those in power. It is hard to imagine that literate people with easy access to the knowledge we have today would believe, for example, Pharaoh in his supernatural divine nature. Thus, awareness increases the degree of (internal and external) freedom; and this is also because a free decentralized society is more economically efficient (you can read a detailed explanation in my book Anarchocapitalism), which the proponents of centralization often do not know, while it is precisely the knowledge of economics (that is, the acquisition of information) that can lead them to this.

From the above insights, regardless of what we believe, sharing our values and beliefs will lead to freedom rather than unfreedom; either by reassessing something ourselves based on feedback within the dialogue, or by enriching someone else. Sometimes, of course, there is a move away from freedom, but this is not as likely as the opposite process - precisely because information leads to freedom rather than the other way around, as explained in the previous paragraphs; and as we have more and more information at our disposal, it can be assumed that we will continue to move closer to freedom (as we have from the time of the pharaohs through the middle ages to the present day), which I consider a favorable prospect. How can we help it? Share, dialogue; and more generally to do all we can to enrich ourselves and others. In accordance with this belief, not only do I not claim intellectual property for any work, but I also do not condition access to my content (lectures, videos, podcasts or texts, including books) on payment - everything can be found on the Internet for a voluntary contribution; and the amount of entrance fees for conferences and lectures, if I choose any at all, I leave it purely to the discretion of the participants, so that everyone can participate even for free. I am not driven by altruism, but rather by the desire to share information, conduct a dialogue (even with those who do not want or cannot pay), learn and contribute my little bit to the most effective spread of freedom.

name: 19. Practice
text: In this chapter, we will focus on the specific actions of individuals that move our society toward freedom; at the same time, none of them had to compete for votes in elections or convince anyone how to live or not to live. I will describe the different activities of different people in different environments - each completely different, yet all united by the spirit of disobedience. Upon closer examination, we find that they have more in common, which we will discuss further in the next chapter; there I will try to use the examples of such individuals and projects to show how each reader could approach practical freedom in his life. For the greatest possible clarity, I choose initiatives in which I directly participate, actively collaborate with them, or at least receive enough information about them directly from their creators in the long term. I will not write about those that are now (almost or completely) inactive, even though I used to work in them (for example, Freedom of Learning, the Czech and Slovak Ludwig von Mises Institute, the Libertarian Institute, or Prague's Parallel Polis), nor about those that are still active, but I do not know enough about them in depth (the Institute of Liberal Studies, the Liberal Institute, the Paralelní Polis outside of Prague, or countless anarchist or libertarian organizations, agoras, and self-governing schools around the world).

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Hedgehog without a cage
text:
Gabriela Ježková did not want to send "her" children to a school where someone would teach them to listen; in 2014, she preferred to found one herself, where you will not find subordinates or superiors, no formal hierarchy, but on the contrary, equal access to children and adults, and therefore space for self-management. A few years later, she approached me if I would also like to study there; as an ardent theoretician in the field of (un)freedom (and) education, I simply could not refuse such an offer - the opportunity to experience in practice the principles discovered and thought out over the years exceeded all my considerable expectations. Not to mention the fact that Ježek without a cage has become my family after some time, in which I can live freely, be myself, make mistakes and be accepted just the way I am (even with them). Without Ježek (and Gabriela), this book probably wouldn't have been created either, whose ideals I managed to put into words thanks to the experiences gained in this self-directed school (and also thanks to my life with Gabriela, to whom I also owe the constant expansion of the horizons of my disobedience).

But let's start from the beginning. When Gabriela approached me to go to Ježek without a cage to learn, it didn't mean that I could start right away, because she (nor anyone else) can't just decide on something like that; I had the longest job interview in my life - it lasted several days in a row, during which no one wanted anything from me, I was not given any tasks: "Just be with us as you want and need." This tends to be confusing for individuals (we recruit children and adults in the same way) who expect an assignment; I, on the other hand, felt natural about it – I visited a few lessons, offered some myself and spent a pleasant time (including evenings and sleepovers at school) with interesting people. Everyone had the opportunity to stay with me and get to know me a little, because the consensus of all those involved was necessary for my acceptance - if even a single person (be it the founder or a freshman) was against it, in Ježek it is not possible to overrule him from the position of the majority. Anyone (which of course includes adults and children) can suggest that someone join us (in my case it happened to be Gabriela, because we knew each other); however, we all decide on acceptance together.

We don't just seek consensus for accepting new hedgehogs; on the contrary, we use it to condition every decision that at least one of us considers important. No one is obliged to participate in the process (everything in Ježek - including attendance - is voluntary), but those who participate will be given the opportunity to express (in addition to other options) a "big yes" or "big no" for any proposal - and these are irrevocable; if such conflicting voices come together on an issue, we will not close it until we find a solution acceptable to all involved. This journey can be (and sometimes is) quite demanding - time-wise, energetically, emotionally, relationally - but it's so worth it that I wouldn't be afraid to call it one of the basic essences of the Hedgehog; not only thanks to it we all learn to communicate our needs and listen to the needs of others (in a democracy you need to get the majority on your side, so it pays to convince the undecided rather than trying to find common ground with the bearers of opposing opinions, which is, of course, exactly what we need for consensus), but above all everyone strengthens the conviction that (i) their voice matters. It really matters. It is not shouted down by the majority, silenced by a higher authority in the hierarchy, lost in rounding during the tallying of election results, or overlooked because of the wearer's young age. All this is written into each of us (especially in early childhood) as strongly as the compulsion to obey, only with the opposite sign; if we want to live in a truly free society, we need to put aside our fears and allow freedom even for the little ones.

We also make all the rules by consensus decision-making; we have quite a lot of them in Ježek - they make it easier for us to live together. Since we fundamentally reject all punishments (after all, they don't even make much sense in a non-hierarchical environment), there is no sanction for not following any rule; in any case, anyone can question each one, which means that the consensus ceases to apply to it, and a new one must be sought. The rules thus fulfill the role of recommendations or best practices. Everyone who is interested participates in their creation, to the extent that suits him; this results in a relatively strong tendency to follow the rules voluntarily - on the one hand, breaking them is not a "freak" when there is no threat of punishment, but above all they are ours, nobody dictated them to us "from above". Since I have been dealing with polycentric law (i.e. decentralized creation of shared norms "from below") for about twenty years, I visited dozens of schools similar to Ježka with the aim of getting to know their way of creating rules; these observations also confirm the above conclusions. However, following the processes in these schools led me to the surprising discovery that the way the rules are codified also matters significantly. A written record often leads to the fact that, when resolving disputes, attention is focused on their letter rather than their spirit, while oral transmission without a record (that's how we do it in Ježek) not only eliminates this problem, but also enables the disappearance of unnecessary rules by simply forgetting them, which significantly reduces being bound by old rules that have already lost their meaning, but no one noticed.

The basic pillars of Ježek are freedom, responsibility and respect – three sides of the same coin; usually only two are mentioned, we forget about the peripheral one. Since our rules are based on consensus, any of us can challenge them at any time, which we consider desirable. This results, among other things, in the complete voluntariness of all activities (including attendance itself), no prohibitions and equality between children and adults ("teachers" and "students" have an equal voice in deciding anything - no one gives others assignments, grades or other evaluations unless explicitly asked to do so); the absence of formal hierarchies is directly related to this. Such a setting is of course contrary to the valid (adultist) legislation; however, laws can be bent (for example, they impose an obligation to evaluate students; however, nowhere is it written that they cannot receive an evaluation of their own choosing) or violated (for example, I am not allowed to teach children to drive or shoot at a school event; however, their wishes - and of course safety - are more important to me than state regulations), which is precisely the way to achieving freedom, which was discussed in the chapter Liberation: I consider Ježek to be an illustrative example of the anarchist agora, although its members (neither did I before) think so of it, and Gabriela certainly did not set it up with the aim of defying the state or changing society - she just wanted freedom for "her" children.

Certainly not everyone in Ježek considers themselves anarchists; I would even say that we are such a minority. However, I believe that every hedgehog on some level understands how unique, free, respectful and loving space we create together; however, we achieve this - and the protection of our way of life - precisely by following the peaceful anarchist principles of disobedience, autonomy, voluntariness and non-violence. In the end, practice not only confirms the theory, but even leads to it even those who do not know it, or do not agree with it. As much as some people in our school consider the state to be necessary (or even something good) and elections and politics important (although I estimate that there will be perhaps even fewer of them than anarchists), they too perceive the absurdity of the school law and see the evil that following it would bring us. When I talk to them about it, I notice shifts in their attitudes; at least for some of them, over time the fear or feelings of guilt that not following the legislation is something bad is alleviated.

Hedgehog's approach (not only) to children brings remarkable results; especially if they live in a similar environment at home. I don't want to talk now about the results of acquiring the usual school knowledge (although I am convinced that self-directed individuals will certainly not take less of them - rather they are profiled by interests - a detailed analysis, however, goes beyond the purpose of this book), but about contact with one's needs, their expression, communication skills and, above all, self-confidence, which results in a tendency to disobey empty authorities and a natural assumption of responsibility for one's life, which are the best prerequisites for internal (and subsequently external) freedom. Between "our" children and pupils of other schools, where I sometimes give lectures, I perceive vast differences. If I had to generalize and summarize them in a few words, I would probably say that some live for themselves out of love for life and the world, while others try to meet the expectations of others out of fear; there are of course exceptions on both sides, but the overall difference is striking. When I see here all those unique autonomous beings who could have been born in the classic state education system, I feel a great sense in what we do; and gratitude to Gabriela, whom I already consider my hero, because despite all (legislative and other) obstacles, she founded this school - it was the first in the Czech Republic, but many others followed, and today there are already dozens of similar ones.

Freedom, self-management, self-development, sharing - all this and much more means Hedgehog without a cage to me.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Free port
text:
I was told at school that I "can't learn"; and according to what they meant by that, I seriously couldn't do it - I didn't enjoy listening to a rather superficial explanation of a diverse subject in three-quarter-hour blocks and subsequently learning everything by heart. Even then, it was more appropriate for me to always focus on one area of knowledge or a specific problem and to investigate intensively for a long time in depth rather than dividing my attention between different topics. However, of all the ways of learning and educational models - each of which suits someone else - public education forces only a few on everyone, while ignoring the others. That's why I was surprised to realize that maybe I learn most effectively through dialogue; I wrote texts about what interested me, published them on the Internet and discussed them with readers in the comments. Their criticism (sometimes quite harsh and even obscene) served me as fuel for further creation; not only did I improve my writing, communication, argumentation, and logical thinking, but it was even easier for me (compared to babbling) to remember completely arbitrary information. For many years I have published articles on the website of the Ludwig von Mises Institute or on the D-FENS weblog (some of them formed the basis of my first book); until in 2015 I had the idea to start my own web platform called Stoky Svobodneho přístavu.

About a year later, communication with readers inspired me to make videos and start a YouTube channel; the name offered - Freeport Channel. Over time, my work attracted more people who showed interest in lectures on the given topics; and other videos were created from those. I started traveling around the Czech Republic and Slovakia, speaking at conferences, in schools (which I still consider to be one of the most important activities) or in various debates and reached the big media; all this despite open declarations of anarchist positions, which well-known anarchists often avoid in order not to be fooled (whereas authenticity suits me). Thanks to the support of many followers, the Freeport Studio was born over time; in it I still discuss with interesting guests. All these activities require, in addition to the financial support of voluntary donors, also collaborators; and thus the Free Harbor was born - an association whose purpose lies primarily in opening the widest possible dialogue about freedom, which includes anarchy, economics, ethics or the free market, however, over time education has emerged as one of our most important topics.

Free port apparently speaks to an order of magnitude fewer children than state education; nevertheless, I know of hundreds of those who were significantly influenced by him (mainly through the topic of disobedience or the realization that if they don't suit the school and it doesn't have to be them) - I'm still in contact with many of them. In connection with self-directed education, the House of the Free Port was also established; it is an area in the north of Bohemia made up of meadows, a forest, a garden and several buildings, in which a community of people was spontaneously born, organizing various events focused on free learning (originally it was SvobodUm of the association Svoboda učení, in which I worked as one of the creators of this project for several years, until it was finally bought by the Freeport). Although these activities are intended for anyone regardless of age, they naturally arouse increased interest from children and parents, which makes me very happy; anyone who doesn't have to grow up in obedience represents a better chance for a slightly freer society.

From other work, I consider the annual Free Port Conference on various topics related to freedom (we have already organized seven of them), the illegal #ne_disobedience action taking place in the spirit of respect for people and public disrespect for state laws, the candidacy of the Nevolte Urza.cz party in the elections (with the aim of spreading anarchist ideas within the pre-election public debate, but with a binding promise to refuse any political positions without hesitation) to be important or money from the public budget, if we could get any), creating the comic and, last but not least, publishing this book. I am happy when any of this inspires someone or otherwise enriches their life, so I try to spread all the content on the Internet, where it has already found hundreds of thousands of recipients over the years (even if many of them do not agree with it, or are even outraged by it). However, I create mainly to fulfill my own need to learn and grow, which is more important to me than the potential effects on other people (and by extension the whole society) - I consider this insight essential for the next chapter.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Cryptocurrency
text:
In late 2008, a person or group of people under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto defined the protocol for the open-source peer-to-peer payment network Bitcoin; it was launched in January 2009 to initially serve as a toy for a few enthusiasts. A year and a half later, someone used it for a purchase for the first time – programmer Laszlo Hanyecz ordered two pizzas for 10,000 BTC; little did he know at the time that in honor of this transaction, crypto-anarchists would start celebrating May 22nd as "Pizza Day" a few years later. Today, for the same number of bitcoins, we could buy, for example, a large private island with a luxurious palace, a power plant, an airport, a port, a jet, a helicopter, a yacht, and perhaps even a submarine; at the same time, we wouldn't have to worry too much about the budget - there would be enough left over for operating costs for the rest of our lives. Why has the price increased so astronomically? More and more people understand that Bitcoin is a great store of value; far better than any current state currency (which, on the other hand, lose value due to their inflationary nature).

From the point of view of a (crypto)anarchist, I see the absence of any central authority as the most important feature of Bitcoin; it is a decentralized network that anyone can join at any time and start participating in its operation. While records of current account balances are managed by banks (and therefore have the ability to freeze them and the like), all Bitcoin transactions (including the complete history) are simultaneously stored by tens of thousands of computers located around the world; and if by chance someone decides to block my funds, the request for their transfer will simply be handled by another. Bad language people claim that the secret services of some of the great powers may be hiding under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto, which I do not consider very likely; however, the beauty of decentralization is that it's completely irrelevant - even if it were true, the creator of Bitcoin has no actual power over it (and not even a backdoor, since it's open source software).

On the contrary, I consider Bitcoin's greatest weakness to be that it is not fully anonymous; although it does not show who owns which funds, but their transfers can be tracked - the history of all transactions is public (although they cannot be linked to specific people without additional information, states are gradually beginning to spend more and more resources to obtain this "additional information"). Although this problem can be solved in most cases and privacy can be protected, it requires an advanced level of understanding of the functioning of the entire network as well as blockchain analysis tools; not to mention the fact that anyone can simply make mistakes, which unfortunately has led to many seasoned crypto-anarchists knowing the inside of a prison cell. In response to this, for example, the Monero project was created - it can be imagined as the "younger brother" of Bitcoin, which, however, operates in complete anonymity and no one can monitor third-party transactions in it without the permission of their author; this is also why it is commonly used on illegal darknet markets (although it has other limitations). For the sake of completeness, I state that Bitcoin has tens of thousands of different "siblings"; almost without exception, these are dysfunctional or outright fraudulent projects, in which you can easily drown your savings - but their existence represents the much-needed competition that separates the wheat from the chaff (and some of them I still consider more trustworthy than national currencies).

When I wrote the chapter on money in my book Anarcho-Capitalism in 2013, I didn't mention Bitcoin in it; although I knew of its existence, its amazing potential remained hidden from me at that time (for about two years). Far more prudent was my friend Slush; in late 2010, he came up with the world's first implementation of a mining pool (i.e. software used for mass confirmation of transactions in the network) and subsequently in 2014 with the so-called Trezor - the world's first hardware wallet (i.e. a device capable of securely storing bitcoins). I don't know who Satoshi Nakamoto was or why he did what he did; However, Slush told me about his motivations - he developed these technologies initially for his own use, because he enjoyed it. Later, his companies broke through on the world market and their products helped millions of people (including me) expand the boundaries of financial freedom for just a few (thousand) crowns; however, this probably did not even occur to him in the early days of discovering Bitcoin - we will return to this observation in the next chapter.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Cryptoanarchy
text:
Cryptocurrencies, however, are only the publicly known tip of the huge iceberg born of crypto-anarchism; this term was first used by Timothy Christopher May in his Cryptoanarchist Manifesto, which he extended to the cypherpunk community as early as 1988. The message of this manifesto is that strong asymmetric cryptography can weaken state power; and not politically, but technologically - politicians can write laws, but the mathematics of encryption algorithms will not obey them. Before the technology of the web, Timothy C. May predicted a world in which we would be able to communicate and trade anonymously, transfer funds outside the banking system and enter into contracts without official identity; all this came true within a few decades. In 1994, he described cryptoanarchy as the practical realization of anarcho-capitalism in cyberspace. I completely agree with that, I would just clarify the statement - in my opinion, this is specifically the realization of anarcho-agorisism, as it is created "from below" uncontrolled by anyone without any central plan or political will.

Today's crypto-anarchists have an abundance of technology at their disposal, from various algorithms to computer networks to very powerful hardware; as a result, they are able to form communities in cyberspace with relative ease. While in the past one could hardly be a member of a tribe without a physical presence, current technologies allow us to do so, allowing a return to (cy)tribalism; at the same time, tribes do not have to exist only virtually - they are often connected to a specific location in the material world (I myself belong to agoras that are physically separated by hundreds of kilometers, so I live in several places, I travel between them, but thanks to the Internet I still participate in their functioning). Such relationships (personal, creative, educational, business, professional, advisory, supportive, charitable, and others) reinforce the decentralization of society; especially if they are followed by individuals who do not require the supervision of external authorities over their lives - they can then interact autonomously and freely in the privacy ensured by cryptography (and, if necessary, in pseudonymity or complete anonymity) without excessive risk of retribution from the state.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Rainbow Family of Living Light
text:
Rainbow Family was formed in 1970 as one of the offshoots of the hippie movement at the American music festival Vortex I (it was a smaller Oregonian version of the well-known Woodstock). Today it is a worldwide informal, non-hierarchical organization numbering probably hundreds of thousands of people (there is no official list of members, but at some meetings tens of thousands have appeared at once). Their basic values are love, peace, freedom, voluntariness, respect for man and nature, spiritual openness, sharing and equality (in the sense of humanity, not necessarily property or other egalitarianism); in accordance with these values, they have no leaders, so they operate in non-violent decentralized self-governments. They decide on all matters by consensus, which sometimes takes a long time with a large number of people; however, it brings (similarly to the Hedgehog without a cage) a number of advantages - above all, a real solution to problems in peace without suppressing those whose voices are not strong enough.

Rainbow Family's most visible events are the Rainbow Gatherings; these are held in nature all over the world and last a month (starting at the new moon, peaking at the full moon and ending at the next new moon). At any given moment, a Rainbow Gathering is taking place somewhere in the world (often in multiple places at the same time); some members of this family move from one meeting to another, so that it constitutes their entire life, others spend part of the year, others arrive occasionally. As part of such an event, for example, thousands of people gather in one (carefully selected) place - Rainbow Family explorers talk to the locals ahead of time, inform them about the gathering and find out their opinions (in case of negative responses, they look for another place); if the given piece of nature has a private owner, his consent is an insurmountable condition. On public (state) land, the permit doesn't matter that much; this sometimes leads to police interventions of varying degrees and intensity, to which the (often naked) hippies always react in the same way - they treat the intervening policemen as rainbow sisters and brothers (they treat everyone who comes to the Rainbow Gathering this way), which sometimes leads to a resolution of the conflict through non-violent communication, other times to a complete cleanup of the area by police force, more often to its closure (but guarding kilometers of dense forest for a month is neither a simple task for dozens of patrols, so it is easy to slip in and out, which Gabriela and I once experienced firsthand in Germany). However, such interventions are quite exceptional; it's typically a peaceful gathering of peaceful hippies who celebrate the full moon, clean up carefully after themselves (there's a lot of emphasis on that) and scatter to all corners of the world (or to the next gathering). They don't need permission to live their own way; they don't even fight anyone for it - they just do it.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Liberation Travel
text:
About ten years ago, a smiling digital nomad, (crypto)anarchist, voluntarist and ethical hacker Pavol "Wilder" Lupták appeared in my life; our meetings and conversations are a great inspiration to me not only for his unfailing good-natured warmth and kindness, but also for his flagrant disobedience to the imposed authorities, to whom he essentially shows a metaphorical raised middle finger throughout his life (with his own peacefulness and kindness, but completely unyielding). Palo likes to travel; and on his travels he noticed significant differences in the approach of individual states to "their" citizens in various areas, which he decided to use to his advantage - somewhere he arranged citizenship, elsewhere tax residence for his company, somewhere else permanent residence, while he pays for his health insurance with a private global insurance company. As a result, his children don't even have to go to school legally, the authorities don't see him very well because he's always moving, and it's not exactly easy to collect taxes on him (among other things because he uses crypto more than state currencies, especially the anonymous Monero); however, I'm pretty sure that his motivation is not greed (on the contrary, he generously helps those in need), but a desire for freedom and autonomy.

When he began to share his knowledge with others, he inspired many anarchists (and other free-spirited people) so much that they decided to follow in his footsteps. Palo did not hesitate and founded Liberation Travel – a professional agency that will arrange permanent residence (and eventually citizenship) for you in, for example, Panama, Uruguay or Paraguay, thereby freeing you from a lot of taxes in Europe or the USA, or setting up a bank account in Georgia or Kyrgyzstan, which does not report bank data to the financial authorities of other countries. I love that even though Liberation Travel understandably charges to deal with red tape, Palo still constantly shares all the necessary information completely free of charge to help people live freely; he himself makes full use of all these services all the time, so he follows legislative changes in the relevant countries and elsewhere on his travels, to which he not only reacts, but also continuously publishes his findings free of charge online and at various conferences around the world. Even this anarchist did not set out on a mission to save the world or society; he simply loves travel and found his way to freedom in it - and then offered it to others.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Students for Liberty
text: Students for Liberty is – as the name suggests – a libertarian student organization; was established in 2008 at a conference of the same name in New York, from where it quickly spread not only to the United States - today it unites over ten thousand students in more than a thousand cells practically all over the world. Their members work together to organize lectures, conferences, debate evenings and informal meetings; they also publish books, but if necessary, they do not hesitate to help their members and their loved ones flee from war-torn areas. The Czech branch was founded in 2013 in Brno, from where it expanded to many other cities; and since the domestic libertarian community is one of the most active on a global scale (and, in terms of population, the largest), it is not so surprising that Students for Liberty CZ won the award for the best student group in the SFL Awards. I have been working with many of their members for many years, we help each other (for example, with the promotion of this book, but also, for example, with hiding persons persecuted by the foreign police). They are typically kind-hearted and respectful young people who enjoy listening, talking, reading and writing about freedom, so they have created a platform to do so. I am extremely happy to perform at the events organized by this organization, because they take place in a very friendly and loving atmosphere full of understanding and tolerance even for different opinions; I don't feel any pressure from the participants to change (either specific individuals or the whole society), on the contrary, rather humility and a desire to expand their own horizons.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Agora
text:
One of the Prague agoras is simply called Agora by its members; although I'm a big fan of names that are as descriptive as possible, I find this one slightly confusing. However, its activities encompass a fairly broad spectrum of freedom-related activities – both in the physical and digital worlds; and as I appreciate both the variety and the independence of these manifestations of disobedience, I will briefly introduce each of them.

The idea that most interested me at the Agora is the linking of anarchists of various directions - from anarcho-capitalists to anarcho-communists - on a common basis, which we hope to gradually find in anarcho-agorism. I believe that in this "middle" could meet all those who are willing to prioritize their anarchist ideals over hostility towards excessive otherness, which they are often not even willing to understand. I myself have been trying unsuccessfully for a similar dialogue among anarchists for many years; and I would very much like the key to it to lie in this very agora.

Another contribution of these anarchists to freedom is the project they also called Agora (probably to avoid confusion). It is a decentralized protocol for the digital representation of relationships and events (in and between agoras), which enables their manifestation in the online environment without the involuntary sharing of data or the need for a central authority. For this, it uses asymmetric cryptography and blockchain technology, which in recent years, when it gained popularity, is very often implemented senselessly - however, I find its use in Agora to be functional, since its creators take into account the so-called "oracle problem"; understandably, they cannot fully solve the problem, but they greatly mitigate its effects. For those who find this paragraph too technical, they can think of the Agora as an encrypted "app" through which members of different agoras can communicate with each other and with each other, plan, trade, make agreements and do a lot of other things, since each agora has the ability to adapt this "app" to its needs without losing the ability to communicate with others. As Agora isn't quite finished yet, I'm not sure if it will come out before or after this book; however, I find its development team to be quite open (they were happy to accept my suggestions and comments on their work) - if you feel like it, you can try to get involved as well.

In addition, Agora also manages the Autonomous Center 254 in Prague's Holešovice; it is a space for individuals and collectives that resonate with anarchist ideas. It brings together a diverse range of individuals from Bitcoiners to artists to the Salvation Army; AC254 members emphasize solidarity, which is manifested, among other things, in the voluntary prices for food and drink that can be obtained and purchased there. I personally like to go to the "two-five-four" to talk about interesting topics related to freedom, but it also hosts various educational and cultural events; I fell in love with the place and the people in it quite quickly - although we don't always agree on everything, they are open to dialogue and, above all, I strongly feel that far more than the (il)legality of any action is solved by its (il)correctness, which is a setting that allows building a truly autonomous space.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Smugglers, dealers, prostitutes and other free outlaws
text:
There are a number of services or commodities on which states impose special taxes or outlaw them altogether; these are mostly foreign goods, drugs, weapons, sex and the like. The original (and often current) reasons for such restrictions are typically related to the centralization of power, the fulfillment of public budgets, (not only pre-election) populism, or even racism. However bizarre or conspiratorial it may sound today, for example, the history of drug prohibition dates back to the nineteenth century, when politicians did not hesitate to play the racist card quite openly; if you look up anything about the origins of the prohibition of cocaine, opium, marijuana, and especially peyote, you might be surprised. Today, the existence of identical regulations is commonly defended on the grounds of health or safety, even where these arguments have no chance of standing deeper than at first glance (which I discuss in detail in the book Anarchocapitalismus and in the lectures on drugs and weapons, the recording of which can be found on the Freeport Channel on YouTube or Odysee). However, the vast majority of people understandably do not have the time or motivation to investigate the meaningfulness of these measures in more depth, so in connection with them, they automatically adopt state positions and justifications portraying the given restrictions as necessary and beneficial to society.

As a result of these majority opinions, everyone who, contrary to valid legislation, supplies others with the goods they demand is then universally condemned; and not so much depending on the real danger of the item in question, but above all according to society-wide prejudices - distributors of any illegal drugs are often blamed by all kinds of moralists with gusto for the negative effects of their goods on the health of consumers, but in my life I have never come across someone blaming a pub or a clerk in a convenience store for alcoholic liver cirrhosis. Of course, among smugglers and dealers (not only drugs) we also find a lot of real criminals who do not shy away from stealing or otherwise restricting the rights and freedoms of others. In addition, purely statistically, we will meet them in these professions more often than in the rest of the population, as the very illegality of their business deters, for example, individuals with a strong aversion to risk or a high need for social recognition (there will be fewer thieves, aggressors, etc. among them precisely because of these characteristics). However, this does not change the fact that even a number of decent and honest people, who do not rob or harm anyone in any other way, make a living by selling drugs, (untaxed) sex and other taboo or outright illegal ways; however, society looks down on them.

These individuals then, as a result of social pressures, often consider themselves outcasts; often they too (due, among other things, to the need to hide their work) eventually come to believe that they are doing something wrong, although they are often just supplying people with goods and services they are interested in. Their biggest "offense" typically consists either in the fact that they sell something that, according to politicians, they should not sell (even in the case of goods with negligible or negative harm), or in the fact that they refuse to share any profits with the state authorities, or they simply do not want to submit to their requirements to comply with meaningless standards or bureaucracy. However, if they take this path (perhaps out of selfish motivations), in my eyes, they are moving our society towards freedom. I am happy for everyone who finds the courage to do his work without permission, regardless of legislation, without taking part of the profit to the state and is guided only by the desire to improve himself or others (with respect to them). Thanks to technology, such individuals can now even meet anonymously on darknet markets; these tend to be a thorn in the side (and the target of aggression) of governments all over the world, as they weaken their power by allowing people to get comfortably and in good quality many things that the state authorities would like to usurp a monopoly over.

I regard all honest smugglers, dealers, whores (I use the word with great respect and appreciation) and other free outlaws as important allies on the road to practical anarchy; I respect them for their disobedience and willingness to live autonomously in their own way regardless of the demands of authority. I let them know this attitude of mine, so then they are typically not shy about talking about their work (including its illegal aspects) in front of me. This is usually a great springboard for introducing them to the relevant knowledge of the Austrian school of economics or various anarchist theories, which they mostly like to listen to - thanks to them, they can see their actions as a useful service to others, not as a reprehensible scumbag at someone's expense, as the state shamefully pushes them to do. I know personally (and in some cases very well) a lot of traffickers in illegal goods and sex workers in the gray economy; many of them were ashamed of their source of livelihood for various reasons, sometimes even so much so that they planned to earn some money and start making an "honorable" living. However, thanks to the understanding of the principles of anarchoagoris (and the support of other like-minded people), these plans were sometimes abandoned. The purpose of some agoras may also be to help their members feel accepted in a world that unfortunately rejects most of them - just as they are. On the way to freedom, we do not only encounter legislative obstacles; we often have to deal with prejudices and social norms as well.

name: 20. Participation
text:
For many years that I have been spreading the idea of freedom in the public space, from time to time (and I am glad that it is becoming more and more often) people come to me with the following prompt: "Okay, Urza, after careful consideration, I agree that I do not need any rulers; but we live in the here and now. What does it mean to me that the state is depriving me of my freedom? It is happening with and without my knowledge. What can I realistically do about it?" The purpose of this book is to answer just such questions. In its first part, I describe how and why we are losing our freedom; the following is an analysis of the paths that do not lead to its reacquisition; however, the previous chapter is the longest of all - it records the specific activities of individual people, thanks to which they themselves (and subsequently others) can live more freely. Let's learn something from them. How are their stories different? And what do they have in common?

The protagonists of our practical examples come from completely different backgrounds and live, at first glance, completely different lives - from mothers with children to (digital) creators, (crypto)anarchists, hackers, but also hippies to dealers and whores (I still use that word with great respect and appreciation). So what unites them? Certainly the desire for freedom, of which they had less than they needed at the beginning of their journey; whether it was the obligation to send one's children to a terrible state school, the monopoly of central banks on money, the necessity to pay taxes or the illegality of some goods or services.
